title: Diverse Why-Provenance for Datalog Queries

paper.title: Diverse Why-Provenance for Datalog Queries
paper.abstract:
Abstract. Datalog is a powerful rule-based language that allows us to express complex recursive queries and has found numerous applications over the years. Explaining why a result to a Datalog query is obtained is an essential task towards explainable and transparent data-intensive applications that rely on Datalog. A standard way of explaining a query result is the so-called why-provenance, which provides information about the witnesses to
a query result in the form of subsets of the input database that as a whole can be used to derive that result.
The state-of-the-art approach for efficiently computing the why-provenance explanations of a certain query result aims at enumerating, without repetitions, the relevant explanations by relying on off-the-shelf SAT solvers.
However, whenever the set of explanations is very large, outputting the entire set might be prohibitively expensive. Moreover, it is questionable the practical usefulness of flooding the user with a very large number of explanations, many of them possibly differing only marginally.
In this case, one can argue that it would be practically more useful to compute a small, sufficiently diverse subset of the set of why-provenance explanations.
The present work initiates the study of the latter problem. In particular, we formalize the problem of interest as an optimization problem, and, after showing that it is highly intractable (it is NP-hard even in data complexity), we investigate whether ILP optimization solvers can be employed towards practical solutions.
Our main finding is that this is achievable as long as we keep the requested set of explanations small, or we employ approximation algorithms (with error guarantees).

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Datalog has emerged in the 1980s as a logic-based query language from Logic Programming and has been extensively studied since then ( Abiteboul et al., 1995 ) . It essentially extends the language of unions of conjunctive queries, which corresponds to the select-project-join-union fragment of relational algebra, with the important feature of recursion, much needed to express some natural queries. As for any other query language, explaining why a result to a Datalog query is obtained is crucial towards explainable and transparent data-intensive applications. A standard way for providing such explanations to query answers is, among others, the so-called why-provenance ( Buneman et al., 2001 ) . Its essence is to collect all the subsets of the input database that as a whole can be used to derive a certain answer. More precisely, in the case of Datalog queries, the why-provenance of an answer tuple t ¯ \bar{t} is obtained by considering all the possible proof trees T T of the fact Ans ​ ( t ¯ ) \text{\rm Ans}(\bar{t}) , with Ans being the answer predicate of the Datalog query in question, and then collecting all the database facts that label the leaves of T T . Recall that a proof tree of a fact α \alpha w.r.t. a database D D and a set Σ \Sigma of Datalog rules forms a tree-like representation of a derivation process that, starting from D D and executing the rules occurring in Σ \Sigma , produces α \alpha ( Abiteboul et al., 1995 ) . Despite its wide acceptance in theory with numerous theoretical studies (see, e.g., ( Calautti et al., 2024c ; Calautti et al., 2024a ; Damásio et al., 2013 ; Deutch et al., 2014 ; Khamis et al., 2022 ) ), why-provenance for Datalog queries suffers from a crucial weaknesses, namely it is computationally very expensive. This is revealed by the fact that until 2020, although why-provenance for Datalog queries has been proposed decades ago, only a couple of works have considered implementing it for recursive queries ( Zhao et al., 2020 ; Esparza et al., 2014 ) . The more recent work ( Elhalawati et al., 2022 ) by Elhalawati et al. tried to make further progress by focusing on the more practical setting of computing the why-provenance of a given query answer (a.k.a. on-demand why-provenance), instead of computing the why-provenance for all the query answers as done in ( Zhao et al., 2020 ; Esparza et al., 2014 ) . Inspired by ( Elhalawati et al., 2022 ) and the idea of on-demand why-provenance, the authors of ( Calautti et al., 2024b ) pushed the state of affairs even further by focusing on the task of enumerating, without repetitions, the members of why-provenance of a given answer by relying on off-the-shelf SAT solvers. In other words, the approach of ( Calautti et al., 2024b ) builds the why-provenance of a query answer in an incremental fashion, i.e., one explanation at a time, which is much more useful in practice than the one-shot computation of the whole set as done in ( Elhalawati et al., 2022 ) . Furthermore, the authors of ( Calautti et al., 2024b ) attacked another weakness of why-provenanance for Datalog queries, namely it might provide counterintuitive explanations. Indeed, as it has been observed in the literature, there are proof trees that correspond to unnatural derivation processes, e.g., derivations where an atom is derived from itself ( Bourgaux et al., 2022 ) , and it is fair to say that an explanation witnessed via such an unnatural proof tree can be classified as a counterintuitive one as it does not correspond to an intuitive derivation process that can be extracted from the proof tree; this is further discussed in Section 3 . Towards conceptually meaningful explanations, the authors of ( Calautti et al., 2024b ) introduced the class of unambiguous proof trees that, unlike arbitrary proof trees, correspond to conceptually meaningful derivation processes, which in turn ensure the conceptual relevance of the obtained explanations. The essence underlying unambiguous proof trees is that they eliminate any ambiguity on how a certain fact α \alpha is derived, namely α \alpha is derived in a unique way that can be exctracted from its unambiguous proof tree. To the best of our knowledge, the approach of ( Calautti et al., 2024b ) forms the state-of-the-art concerning the effective compution of on-demand why-provenance, with the experimental evaluation of ( Calautti et al., 2024b ) providing very encouraging results. Having said that, it remains questionable the practical usefuleness of flooding the user with an extremely large number of why-provenance explanations of the answer of interest, many of them possibly differing only marginally. One can argue that whenever the set of why-provenance explanations of an answer gets very large, it would be practically more useful to provide an overview by outputting a “representative” subset of the set of explanations. A general discussion on this matter about arbitary problems (not only about on-demand why-provenance) can be found in ( Merkl et al., 2025 ) . Two ways for computing a “representative” subset of the set of why-provenance explanations are the following: Sampling Approach.: Randomly select explanations, similarly to what was done for the problem of computing answers to conjunctive queries ( Arenas et al., 2021 ; Carmeli et al., 2022 ) . Diversity Approach.: Conpute a small “diverse” subset of the set of explanations, similarly to what was done for the problem of computing answers to conjunctive queries ( Arenas et al., 2025 ; Merkl et al., 2025 ) . The present work initiates the study of the problem of computing a “representative” subset of the set of why-provenance explanations by adopting the diversity approach. Let us stress that the diversity approach has been applied to numerous problems related to databases (see, e.g., ( Arenas et al., 2025 ; Deng and Fan, 2014 ; Fan et al., 2024 ; Merkl et al., 2025 ) ) and symbolic AI (see, e.g., ( Eiter et al., 2013 ; Hebrard et al., 2005 ; Ingmar et al., 2020 ; Petit and Trapp, 2015 ) ). Following what was done in the literature in other contexts ( Ingmar et al., 2020 ; Merkl et al., 2025 ) , to properly define our problem of interest, we first need to fix the notion of distance between any two why-provenance explanations and the notion of diversity measure that acts as an aggregator that combines pairwise distances. Having those two notions in place, our problem is naturally defined as an optimization problem that aims to compute a set { D 1 , … , D k } \{D_{1},\ldots,D_{k}\} of k k why-provenance explanations (if such a set exists), for some k > 0 k>0 specifed by the user, that maximizes the value obtained by aggregating, using the diversty measure, the pairwise distances of the computed explanations D 1 , … , D k D_{1},\ldots,D_{k} . Concerning the distance between explanations, we adopt the symmetric difference distance, that is, the number of facts on which two explanations D ′ D^{\prime} and D ′′ D^{\prime\prime} differ, denoted by d ⁡ ( D ′ , D ′′ ) d(D^{\prime},D^{\prime\prime}) . Recall that a why-provenance explanation is a subset of the given database (and thus, a set of facts), which means that we can refer to the symmetric difference of D ′ D^{\prime} and D ′′ D^{\prime\prime} . In other words, d ⁡ ( D ′ , D ′′ ) d(D^{\prime},D^{\prime\prime}) is the cardinality of the set of facts ( D ′ ∖ D ′′ ) ∪ ( D ′′ ∖ D ′ ) (D^{\prime}\setminus D^{\prime\prime})\cup(D^{\prime\prime}\setminus D^{\prime}) . When it comes to the diversity measure, in general, one can adopt any computable function f f of the form ⋃ k > 0 ℕ k ⁡ ( k − 1 ) 2 → ℝ \bigcup_{k>0}\mathbb{N}^{\frac{k(k-1)}{2}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} , that is, a function that, for each k > 0 k>0 , assigns to each tuple of integers ( d 1 , … , d k ⁡ ( k − 1 ) 2 ) \left(d_{1},\ldots,d_{\frac{k(k-1)}{2}}\right) , which are essentially the pairwise distances of k k why-provenance explanations, a real number. Of course, towards practical solutions to our problem of interest, the function f f should be conceptually relevant and efficiently computable (i.e., computable in polynomial time). Concrete such functions that have been considered in the literature are, for example, the sum and min functions that assign to a tuple of integers ( d 1 , … , d k ⁡ ( k − 1 ) 2 ) \left(d_{1},\ldots,d_{\frac{k(k-1)}{2}}\right) the integer d 1 + ⋯ + d k ⁡ ( k − 1 ) 2 d_{1}+\cdots+d_{\frac{k(k-1)}{2}} and min ⁡ { d 1 , … , d k ⁡ ( k − 1 ) 2 } \min\left\{d_{1},\ldots,d_{\frac{k(k-1)}{2}}\right\} , respectively ( Merkl et al., 2025 ) . In this work, we adopt the sum function as one of the most commonly used diversity measures. We can now give a semi-formal definition of the optimization problem of interest; the formal definition is given in Section 4 : PROBLEM : 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} INPUT : A Datalog query Q Q , a database D D , an answer t ¯ {\bar{t}} to Q Q over D D , and an integer k > 0 k>0 OUTPUT : A set { D 1 , … , D k } \{D_{1},\ldots,D_{k}\} of why-provenance explanations of t ¯ \bar{t} w.r.t. D D and Q Q that maximizes ∑ 1 ≤ i < j ≤ k d ⁡ ( D i , D j ) \sum_{1\leq i<j\leq k}d(D_{i},D_{j}) if it exists; otherwise fail The goal of the present work is to study the above problem with the aim of providing effective solutions that can be used in practice. For the sake of completeness, we are interested in both settings where the explanations are obtained from arbitary or unambiguous proof trees. Recall that unambiguous proof trees have been introduced in ( Calautti et al., 2024b ) and correspond to conceptually meaningful derivations processes, which in turn lead to conceptually relevant explanations. The first research question that comes up concerns the complexity of 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} : Question 1. Is 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} tractable or intractable? Our theoretical analysis reveals that we are dealing with a highly intractable optimization problem. In particular, we show that our problem is NP-hard, no matter which class of proof trees we consider (arbitrary or unambiguous), even if the Datalog query is fixed (i.e., in data complexity) and consists of a single Datalog rule. This suggests that for providing practical solutions to our problem we need to exploit existing optimization methods that are able to deal with NP-hard problems. A natural choice is Integer Linear Programming (ILP), which leads to our second research question: Question 2. Can ILP optimization solvers lead to practical solutions for 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} ? The key idea towards an answer to the above question is to cast 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} as an ILP optimization problem Π \Pi in such a way that each diverse set of interest can be exctracted from an optimal solution of Π \Pi . Since there are mutliple ways of achieveing this, we define a general framework that allows us to devise such ILP optimization problems in a uniform way, and present a generic algorithm that exploits this framework for solving our problem. The main technical ingredient of this framework is the notion of ILP encoding of the why-provenance explanations of a query answer, which is essentially a system T T of ILP constraints such that each why-provenance explanation of the answer of interest can be extracted from a solution of T T . Given an ILP encoding T T of some query answer and an integer k > 0 k>0 , we then define the ILP optimization problem Π ⁡ [ T , k ] \Pi[T,k] such that each diverse set of k k why-provenance explanations of the answer to be explained can be extracted from an optimal solution of Π ⁡ [ T , k ] \Pi[T,k] . Thus, any pair ( T , k ) (T,k) , where T T is an ILP encoding of some answer and k > 0 k>0 some integer, immediately leads to the ILP optimization problem Π ⁡ [ T , k ] \Pi[T,k] . Now, once we fix our preferred way of building the ILP encoding, we immediately get an algorithm that solves 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} . In particular, given a Datalog query Q Q , a database D D , an answer t ¯ \bar{t} to Q Q over D D , and an integer k k , the algorithm (i) constructs the ILP optimization problem Π ⁡ [ T , k ] \Pi[T,k] , where T T is build according to the fixed preferred way, (ii) finds an optimal solution μ \mu of Π ⁡ [ T , k ] \Pi[T,k] if it exists (otherwise, it fails) by calling an off-the-shelf ILP optimization solver, and (iii) returns the diverse set of k k why-provenance explanations of t ¯ \bar{t} that can be exctracted from the solution μ \mu of Π ⁡ [ T , k ] \Pi[T,k] . After experimenting with different ILP encodings, we have observed that providing practical solutions to 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} is attainable, no matter whether the explanations are obtained from arbitary or unambiguous proof trees, as long as we ask for small diverse sets of explanations (i.e., when the diversity parameter k k is at most three). On the other hand, all the considered ILP encodings lead to algorithms that exhibit poor scalability w.r.t. the diversity parameter k k , and thus, quickly become infeasible for computing larger diverse sets of explanations. This brings us to our last research question whether we can devise alternative approaches that trade optimality of the computed diverse sets for performamce: Question 3. Can we devise approximation algorithms (with error guarantees) for 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} that perform much faster than the exact algorithms and can deal with larger diverse sets? Towards this direction, we target 2 2 -approximation algorithms for 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} that accept as input a Datalog query Q Q , a database D D , an answer t ¯ \bar{t} to Q Q over D D , and an integer k > 0 k>0 , and produce a set { D 1 ′ , … , D k ′ } \{D^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,D^{\prime}_{k}\} of why-provenance explanations of t ¯ \bar{t} (assuming it exists; otherwise, the algorithm fails) such that ∑ 1 ≤ i < j ≤ k d ⁡ ( D i ′ , D j ′ ) ≥ 1 2 ⋅ ∑ 1 ≤ i < j ≤ k d ⁡ ( D i , D j ) , \sum_{1\leq i<j\leq k}d(D^{\prime}_{i},D^{\prime}_{j})\ \geq\ \frac{1}{2}\cdot\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq k}d(D_{i},D_{j}), where { D 1 , … , D k } \{D_{1},\ldots,D_{k}\} is a set of explanations with maximal diversity, i.e., it maximizes ∑ 1 ≤ i < j ≤ k d ⁡ ( D i , D j ) \sum_{1\leq i<j\leq k}d(D_{i},D_{j}) . Similarly to the exact solutions discussed above, we use the generic framework for constructing ILP optimization problems, which in turn are based on the notion of ILP encoding of the why-provenance explanations of a query answer, to devise a generic 2 2 -approximation algorithm for 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} . After experimenting with the various ILP encodings that underly our exact algorithms, we have concluded that the approximation algorithms are indeed much faster than the exact ones with the runtime being reduced by several orders of magnitude. Even as the diversity parameter k k increases, runtimes remain low, with the vast majority of runs completing well below one second, which is a significant improvement over the exact algorithms. We have also assessed the quality of the approximation algorithms and observed that the approximation ratios remain quite close to one. This tells us that the approximation ratios achieved in practice are generally much better than the theoretical ones. Roadmap. After introducing some preliminary notions in Section 2 and the basics of why-provenace for Datalog in Section 3 , we formally define the optimization problem of interest and analyze its data complexity in Section 4 . The general framework for devising ILP optimization problems, as well as the generic algorithm for 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} , are presented in Section 5 . The various ILP encodings of why-provenance are given in Section 6 . The experimental evaluation of the exact algorithms is performed and discussed in Section 7 . The generic 2 2 -approximation algorithm for 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} is presented in Section 8 . The experimental evaluation of the approximation algorithms is performed and discussed in Section 9 . We finally conclude in Section 10 . The source code and datasets used in our experimental evaluation can be found at https://github.com/mostafamilani/datalog-div-prov.

sections.heading: 2. Preliminaries
sections.text: We consider the disjoint countably infinite sets 𝐂 \mathbf{C} and 𝐕 \mathbf{V} of constants and variables , respectively. We may refer to constants and variables as terms . For an integer n > 0 n>0 , we write [ n ] [n] for the set of integers { 1 , … , n } \{1,\ldots,n\} . In what follows, we adopt the terminology and notation from the recent work ( Calautti et al., 2024c ) , where the data complexity of why-provenance for Datalog queries has been studied. Relational Databases. A schema 𝐒 \mathbf{S} is a finite set of relation names (or predicates) with associated arity. We write R / n R/n to say that R R has arity n ≥ 0 n\geq 0 ; we may also write 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \mathsf{ar}(R) for n n . A (relational) atom α \alpha over 𝐒 \mathbf{S} is an expression of the form R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) R(\bar{t}) , where R / n ∈ 𝐒 R/n\in\mathbf{S} and t ¯ \bar{t} is an n n -tuple of terms. By abuse of notation, we may treat tuples as the set of their elements. A fact is an atom with only constants. A database over 𝐒 \mathbf{S} is a finite set of facts over 𝐒 \mathbf{S} . The active domain of a database D D , denoted 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ⁡ ( D ) \mathsf{dom}(D) , is the set of constants in D D . Syntax of Datalog Programs. A (Datalog) rule σ \sigma over a schema 𝐒 \mathbf{S} is an expression of the form R 0 ( x ¯ 0 ) :– R 1 ( x ¯ 1 ) , … , R n ( x ¯ n ) R_{0}(\bar{x}_{0})\,\,\,\text{:--}\,\,\,R_{1}(\bar{x}_{1}),\ldots,R_{n}(\bar{x}_{n}) for n ≥ 1 n\geq 1 , where R i ​ ( x ¯ i ) R_{i}(\bar{x}_{i}) is a (constant-free) relational atom over 𝐒 \mathbf{S} for i ∈ { 0 , … , n } i\in\{0,\ldots,n\} , and each variable in x ¯ 0 \bar{x}_{0} occurs in x ¯ k \bar{x}_{k} for some k ∈ [ n ] k\in[n] . We refer to R 0 ​ ( x ¯ 0 ) R_{0}(\bar{x}_{0}) as the head of σ \sigma , denoted 𝗁𝖾𝖺𝖽 ⁡ ( σ ) \mathsf{head}(\sigma) , and to the expression R 1 ​ ( x ¯ 1 ) , … , R n ​ ( x ¯ n ) R_{1}(\bar{x}_{1}),\ldots,R_{n}(\bar{x}_{n}) as the body of σ \sigma , denoted 𝖻𝗈𝖽𝗒 ⁡ ( σ ) \mathsf{body}(\sigma) , which we may treat as the set of its atoms. A Datalog program over a schema 𝐒 \mathbf{S} is a finite set Σ \Sigma of Datalog rules over 𝐒 \mathbf{S} . A predicate R R occurring in Σ \Sigma is called extensional if there is no rule in Σ \Sigma having R R in its head, and intentional if there is at least one rule in Σ \Sigma with R R in its head. The extensional (database) schema of Σ \Sigma , denoted 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , is the set of all extensional predicates in Σ \Sigma , while the intentional schema of Σ \Sigma , denoted 𝗂𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{idb}(\Sigma) , is the set of all intensional predicates in Σ \Sigma . Note that, by definition, 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) ∩ 𝗂𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) = ∅ \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma)\cap\mathsf{idb}(\Sigma)=\emptyset . The schema of Σ \Sigma , denoted 𝗌𝖼𝗁 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{sch}(\Sigma) , is the set 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) ∪ 𝗂𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma)\cup\mathsf{idb}(\Sigma) , which is in general a subset of 𝐒 \mathbf{S} since some predicates of 𝐒 \mathbf{S} may not appear in Σ \Sigma . Semantics of Datalog Programs. An interesting property of Datalog programs is that their semantics can be equivalently defined in three different ways: model-theoretically, via a fixpoint procedure, and proof-theoretically; see, e.g., ( Abiteboul et al., 1995 ) . We proceed to recall the proof-theoretic semantics of Datalog programs. To this end, we need the key notion of proof tree of a fact, which will anyway play a crucial role in our work. For a database D D and a Datalog program Σ \Sigma , let 𝖻𝖺𝗌𝖾 ⁡ ( D , Σ ) \mathsf{base}(D,\Sigma) be the set that collects all the facts that can be formed using predicates of 𝗌𝖼𝗁 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{sch}(\Sigma) and constants of 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ⁡ ( D ) \mathsf{dom}(D) . D D and Σ \Sigma indicates that we can prove α \alpha using D D and Σ \Sigma , i.e., we can derive α \alpha starting from D D end executing the rules of Σ \Sigma . In fact, there are infinitely many as one can build larger and larger such proof trees: whenever we encounter a node labeled by A ⁡ ( a ) A(a) , we can choose to apply the recursive rule A ( x ) :– A ( y ) , A ( z ) , T ( y , z , x ) A(x)\ \text{:--}\ A(y),A(z),T(y,z,x) . Now, given a Datalog program Σ \Sigma and a database D D over 𝗌𝖼𝗁 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{sch}(\Sigma) , the semantics of Σ \Sigma on D D is the set Σ ⁡ ( D ) = { α ∣ there is a proof tree of ​ α ​ w.r.t. ​ D ​ and ​ Σ } , \Sigma(D)\ =\ \{\alpha\mid\text{ there is a proof tree of }\alpha\text{ w.r.t. }D\text{ and }\Sigma\}, that is, the set of facts that can be proven using D D and Σ \Sigma . Datalog Queries. Having the syntax and the semantics of Datalog programs in place, it is now straightforward to recall the syntax and the semantics of Datalog queries. A Datalog query is a pair Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , where Σ \Sigma is a Datalog program and R R a predicate of 𝗂𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{idb}(\Sigma) . Now, for a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , the answer to Q Q over D D is defined as the set of tuples Q ⁡ ( D ) = { t ¯ ∈ 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) ∣ R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) ∈ Σ ⁡ ( D ) } , Q(D)\ =\ \left\{\bar{t}\in\mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)}\mid R(\bar{t})\in\Sigma(D)\right\}, i.e., all those tuples t ¯ \bar{t} such that the fact R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) R(\bar{t}) can be proven using D D and Σ \Sigma . The class of all the Datalog queries is denoted 𝖣𝖺𝗍 \mathsf{Dat} .

sections.heading: 3. Why-Provenance for Datalog
sections.text: Why-provenance is a standard way of explaining why a query result is obtained. It essentially collects all the subsets of the database that can be used as a whole to prove (or derive) a query result. We proceed to recall the details following ( Calautti et al., 2024c ) . Given a proof tree T = ( V , E , λ ) T=(V,E,\lambda) (of some fact w.r.t. some database and Datalog program), the support of T T is the family of sets of atoms 𝗌𝗎𝗉𝗉𝗈𝗋𝗍 ⁡ ( T ) = { λ ⁡ ( v ) ∣ v ∈ V ​ is a leaf of ​ T } , \mathsf{support}(T)\ =\ \left\{\lambda(v)\mid v\in V\text{ is a leaf of }T\right\}, i.e., the set of facts that label the leaves of the proof tree T T . Note that 𝗌𝗎𝗉𝗉𝗈𝗋𝗍 ⁡ ( T ) \mathsf{support}(T) is a subset of the underlying database since, by definition, the leaves of a proof tree are labeled with database atoms. The formal definition of why-provenance follows. Definition 3.1 ( Why-Provenance for Datalog ). Consider a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , and a tuple t ¯ ∈ 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \bar{t}\in\mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} . The why-provenance of t ¯ \bar{t} w.r.t. D D and Q Q is defined as the family of sets of facts { 𝗌𝗎𝗉𝗉𝗈𝗋𝗍 ⁡ ( T ) ∣ T ​ is a proof tree of ​ R ​ ( t ¯ ) ​ w.r.t. ​ D ​ and ​ Σ } , \{\mathsf{support}(T)\mid T\text{ is a proof tree of }R(\bar{t})\text{ w.r.t. }D\text{ and }\Sigma\}, which we denote by 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⁡ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}(\bar{t},D,Q) . Intuitively, a set of facts D ′ ⊆ D D^{\prime}\subseteq D from 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⁡ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}(\bar{t},D,Q) should be understood as a “real” reason why the tuple t ¯ \bar{t} is an answer to the query Q Q over D D , i.e., D ′ D^{\prime} explains why t ¯ ∈ Q ⁡ ( D ) \bar{t}\in Q(D) . By “real” we mean that all the facts of D ′ D^{\prime} are really used in order to derive the tuple t ¯ \bar{t} as an answer. Here is a simple example of why-provenance. Example 3.2. Let Q = ( Σ , A ) Q=(\Sigma,A) , where Σ \Sigma is the program that encodes the path accessibility problem as in Example 2.2 , and let D D be the database from Example 2.2 . It is easy to verify that the why-provenance of the unary tuple ( d ) (d) w.r.t. D D and Q Q consists of { S ⁡ ( a ) , T ⁡ ( a , a , d ) } \{S(a),T(a,a,d)\} and the database D D itself. The former set is actually the support of the first proof tree given in Example 2.2 , while D D is the support of the second proof tree. Refined Why-Provenance. Although the notion of proof tree introduced above is the standard one used to define the notion of why-provennace for Datalog queries, it has been observed in the literature (see, e.g., ( Bourgaux et al., 2022 ; Calautti et al., 2024c ; Calautti et al., 2024b ) ) that there are counterintuitive proof trees, which in turn lead to counterintuitive explanations based on why-provenance. Such a proof tree is the second one in Example 2.2 that suffers from “ambiguity”. In particular, there are two nodes labeled with A ⁡ ( a ) A(a) , but their subtrees differ, which means that, according to the proof tree in question, it is ambiguous how A ⁡ ( a ) A(a) is derived starting from the database D D . The above observation led to the class of unambiguous proof trees, which essentially forces a fact to be consistently proven via a certain derivation ( Calautti et al., 2024b ) ; see, e.g., the first proof tree in Example 2.2 . To formalize this simple idea we need the notion of isomorphism among rooted trees. Two rooted trees T = ( V , E , λ ) T=(V,E,\lambda) and T ′ = ( V ′ , E ′ , λ ′ ) T^{\prime}=(V^{\prime},E^{\prime},\lambda^{\prime}) are isomorphic , denoted T ≈ T ′ T\approx T^{\prime} , if there is a bijection h : V → V ′ h:V\rightarrow V^{\prime} such that, for each v ∈ V v\in V , λ ⁡ ( v ) = λ ′ ​ ( h ⁡ ( v ) ) \lambda(v)=\lambda^{\prime}(h(v)) , and for each u , v ∈ V u,v\in V , ( u , v ) ∈ E (u,v)\in E iff ( h ⁡ ( u ) , h ⁡ ( v ) ) ∈ E ′ (h(u),h(v))\in E^{\prime} . Let T ⁡ [ v ] T[v] be the subtree of the proof tree T T rooted at node v v . The definition of unambiguous proof trees follows. Definition 3.3 ( Unambiguous Proof Tree ). Consider a Datalog program Σ \Sigma , a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , and a fact α \alpha . An unambiguous proof tree of α \alpha w.r.t. D D and Σ \Sigma is a proof tree T = ( V , E , λ ) T=(V,E,\lambda) of α \alpha w.r.t. D D and Σ \Sigma such that, for all v , u ∈ V v,u\in V , λ ⁡ ( v ) = λ ⁡ ( u ) \lambda(v)=\lambda(u) implies T ⁡ [ v ] ≈ T ⁡ [ u ] T[v]\approx T[u] . Having the notion of unambiguous proof tree in place, we can then refine the notion of why-provenance for Datalog queries by considering only unambiguous proof trees; the formal definition is omitted since it is identical to Definition 3.1 with the difference that we only collect the supports of unambiguous proof trees. Given a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , and a tuple t ¯ ∈ 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \bar{t}\in\mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} , we refer to the why-provenance of t ¯ \bar{t} w.r.t. D D and Q Q relative to unambiguous proof trees , denoted 𝗐𝗁𝗒 𝖴𝖭 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\mathsf{UN}}(\bar{t},D,Q) . To be able to treat in a uniform way the notion of why-provenance relative to arbitrary proof trees (as given in Definition 3.1 ) and the notion of why-provenance relative to unambiguous proof trees, in the rest of the paper we will write 𝗐𝗁𝗒 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) instead of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⁡ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}(\bar{t},D,Q) for the why-provenance of t ¯ \bar{t} w.r.t. D D and Q Q . At this point, let us clarify that why-provenance relative to unambiguous proof trees is indeed a refinement of why-provenance (relative to arbitrary proof trees). Indeed, given a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , and a tuple t ¯ ∈ 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \bar{t}\in\mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} , we have 𝗐𝗁𝗒 𝖴𝖭 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) ⊆ 𝗐𝗁𝗒 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\mathsf{UN}}(\bar{t},D,Q)\subseteq\mathsf{why}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) . Let us stress, however, that this is not the case when it comes to the semantics of Datalog. In other words, whenever there is a proof tree of a fact α \alpha w.r.t. D D and Σ \Sigma , then there is an unambiguous one. This is a desirable property since it implies the following: if t ¯ ∈ Q ⁡ ( D ) \bar{t}\in Q(D) , then 𝗐𝗁𝗒 𝖴𝖭 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) ≠ ∅ \mathsf{why}_{\mathsf{UN}}(\bar{t},D,Q)\neq\emptyset , which is what we expect from an explainability notion for Datalog.

sections.heading: 4. Diverse Why-Provenance
sections.text: As discussed in the Introduction, our goal is, given a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , and a tuple t ¯ ∈ 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) {\bar{t}}\in\mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} , to compute a set of k > 0 k>0 diverse explanations of why t ¯ ∈ Q ⁡ ( D ) \bar{t}\in Q(D) according to the notion of why-provenance (relative to arbitrary or unambiguous proof trees) introduced in the previous section. To formalize this task, we transfer the general diversity framework for query answers from ( Arenas et al., 2024 ) to the setting of why-provenance. Consider a non-empty subset 𝒮 \mathcal{S} of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) , where ⋆ ∈ { 𝖠𝖫𝖫 , 𝖴𝖭 } \star\in\{\mathsf{ALL},\mathsf{UN}\} , if it exists. To determine the diversity of 𝒮 \mathcal{S} , we first determine how different the pairs of databases in 𝒮 \mathcal{S} are. This is done by using their symmetric difference. For two databases D 1 , D 2 ∈ 𝒮 D_{1},D_{2}\in\mathcal{S} , the symmetric difference between D 1 D_{1} and D 2 D_{2} , denoted Δ ⁡ ( D 1 , D 2 ) \Delta(D_{1},D_{2}) , is the set ( D 1 ∖ D 2 ) ∪ ( D 2 ∖ D 1 ) (D_{1}\setminus D_{2})\cup(D_{2}\setminus D_{1}) . We then define the distance between D 1 D_{1} and D 2 D_{2} , written d ⁡ ( D 1 , D 2 ) d(D_{1},D_{2}) , as the integer | Δ ⁡ ( D 1 , D 2 ) | |\Delta(D_{1},D_{2})| . Finally, the diversity of 𝒮 = { D 1 , … , D k } \mathcal{S}=\{D_{1},\ldots,D_{k}\} , denoted δ ⁡ ( 𝒮 ) \delta(\mathcal{S}) , is defined as ∑ i , j ∈ [ k ] ​ and ​ i < j d ⁡ ( D i , D j ) . \sum\limits_{i,j\in[k]\text{ and }i<j}d(D_{i},D_{j}). We are now ready to introduce the main problems of interest. For a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , a tuple t ¯ ∈ 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \bar{t}\in\mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} , and an integer k > 0 k>0 , we write 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ k ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}^{k}(\bar{t},D,Q) , for ⋆ ∈ { 𝖠𝖫𝖫 , 𝖴𝖭 } \star\in\{\mathsf{ALL},\mathsf{UN}\} , to denote the collection of all sets 𝒮 ⊆ 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) with | 𝒮 | = k |\mathcal{S}|=k , i.e., each element of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ k ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}^{k}(\bar{t},D,Q) contains exactly k k members of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) . The main problems of interest are optimization problems that essentially ask to compute a set of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ k ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}^{k}(\bar{t},D,Q) with maximal diversity: PROBLEM : ⋆ - ​ 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \star\text{-}\mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} INPUT : A Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , a tuple t ¯ ∈ 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) {\bar{t}}\in\mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} , and an integer k > 0 k>0 OUTPUT : A member of arg ​ max 𝒮 ∈ 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ k ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) ⁡ δ ​ ( 𝒮 ) \argmax\limits_{\mathcal{S}\in\mathsf{why}_{\star}^{k}(\bar{t},D,Q)}\delta(\mathcal{S}) if it exists; otherwise fail Recall that arg ​ max \argmax refers to the arguments of the maxima with arg ​ max 𝒮 ∈ 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ k ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) δ ( 𝒮 ) = { 𝒮 ∈ 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ k ( t ¯ , D , Q ) ∣ δ ( 𝒮 ′ ) ≤ δ ( 𝒮 ) for each S ′ ∈ 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ k ( t ¯ , D , Q ) } . \argmax\limits_{\mathcal{S}\in\mathsf{why}_{\star}^{k}(\bar{t},D,Q)}\delta(\mathcal{S})\ =\ \left\{\mathcal{S}\in\mathsf{why}_{\star}^{k}(\bar{t},D,Q)\mid\delta(\mathcal{S}^{\prime})\leq\delta(\mathcal{S})\right.\\ \left.\text{ for each }S^{\prime}\in\mathsf{why}_{\star}^{k}(\bar{t},D,Q)\right\}. It is clear that there may be several sets 𝒮 ∈ 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ k ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathcal{S}\in\mathsf{why}_{\star}^{k}(\bar{t},D,Q) with maximal diversity. Our problems simply ask to compute one of those sets. Observe that in the above definition of our problems, all the relevant components are part of the input, but we are also interested in the scenario where the Datalog query is fixed, i.e., for each Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , we are interested in the problem: PROBLEM : ⋆ - ​ 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 ​ [ Q ] \star\text{-}\mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance}[Q] INPUT : A database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , a tuple t ¯ ∈ 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) {\bar{t}}\in\mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} , and an integer k > 0 k>0 OUTPUT : A member of arg ​ max 𝒮 ∈ 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ k ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) ⁡ δ ​ ( 𝒮 ) \argmax\limits_{\mathcal{S}\in\mathsf{why}_{\star}^{k}(\bar{t},D,Q)}\delta(\mathcal{S}) if it exists; otherwise fail We proceed to show that we are dealing with intractable optimization problems, no matter the underlying class of proof trees (arbitrary or unambiguous), even if the Datalog query is fixed and consists of a single Datalog rule. Theorem 4.1. For each ⋆ ∈ { 𝖠𝖫𝖫 , 𝖴𝖭 } \star\in\{\mathsf{ALL},\mathsf{UN}\} , there exists a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , where Σ \Sigma consists of a single Datalog rule, such that ⋆ - ​ 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 ​ [ Q ] \star\text{-}\mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance}[Q] is NP-hard. Theorem 4.1 suggests that for providing practical solutions to our problems we need to exploit existing optimization methods that are able to solve NP-hard problems. We proceed in the next section to discuss how this can be achieved via Integer Linear Programming.

sections.heading: 5. Diverse Why-provenance via Integer Linear Programming
sections.text: We aim to encode ⋆ - ​ 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \star\text{-}\mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} , for ⋆ ∈ { 𝖠𝖫𝖫 , 𝖴𝖭 } \star\in\{\mathsf{ALL},\mathsf{UN}\} , as an Integer Linear Programming (ILP) maximization problem Π \Pi in such a way that each set 𝒮 ∈ 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ k ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathcal{S}\in\mathsf{why}_{\star}^{k}(\bar{t},D,Q) , for some Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , tuple t ¯ ∈ 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \bar{t}\in\mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} , and integer k > 0 k>0 , that maximizes δ ⁡ ( 𝒮 ) \delta(\mathcal{S}) can be extracted from one of the optimal solutions of Π \Pi . Of course, as we shall see in the next section, there are multiple ways to construct such an encoding, relying on different characterizations of when a database D ′ D^{\prime} is a member of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) . Hence, in this section, we first define a general framework for devising such ILP maximization problems in a uniform way, and present a generic algorithm that exploits this framework for solving ⋆ - ​ 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \star\text{-}\mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} . We will then show how to instantiate such an algorithm with concrete encodings. We start by recalling the basics of ILP, and then introduce the key properties that an ILP encoding should enjoy to allow us to cast ⋆ - ​ 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \star\text{-}\mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} as an ILP maximization problem.

sections.heading: 5.1. Integer Linear Programming
sections.text: Consider the disjoint sets X X and B B of integer variables and binary variables, respectively. An ILP constraint over X X and B B is an expression of the form a 1 ​ x 1 + ⋯ + a n ​ x n ⋄ a 0 , a_{1}x_{1}+\cdots+a_{n}x_{n}\ \diamond\ a_{0}, where, for each i ∈ [ n ] i\in[n] , a i ∈ ℚ a_{i}\in\mathbb{Q} , x i ∈ X ∪ B x_{i}\in X\cup B , ⋄ ∈ { ≥ , ≤ , = } \diamond\in\{\geq,\leq,=\} , and a 0 ∈ ℚ a_{0}\in\mathbb{Q} . An assignment for X X and B B is a function μ : X ∪ B → ℤ \mu:X\cup B\rightarrow\mathbb{Z} such that, for each x ∈ B x\in B , μ ⁡ ( x ) ∈ { 0 , 1 } \mu(x)\in\{0,1\} . Such an assignment μ \mu satisfies the constraint a 1 ​ x 1 + ⋯ + a n ​ x n ⋄ a 0 a_{1}x_{1}+\cdots+a_{n}x_{n}\diamond a_{0} over X X and B B if it holds that a 1 ​ μ ​ ( x 1 ) + ⋯ + a n ​ μ ​ ( x n ) ⋄ a 0 . a_{1}\mu(x_{1})+\cdots+a_{n}\mu(x_{n})\diamond a_{0}. A system of ILP constraints over X X and B B is a set T T of ILP constraints over X X and B B . A solution of T T is an assignment for X X and B B that satisfies all the constraints in T T ; we write 𝗌𝗈𝗅 ⁡ ( T ) \mathsf{sol}(T) for the set that collects all the solutions of T T . If T T admits a solution, i.e., 𝗌𝗈𝗅 ⁡ ( T ) ≠ ∅ \mathsf{sol}(T)\neq\emptyset , then we say that T T is feasible ; otherwise, T T is unfeasible . An ILP maximization problem over X X and B B is a pair ( f , T ) (f,T) , where f f , called the objective function , is an expression of the form c 1 ​ z 1 + ⋯ + c m ​ z m c_{1}z_{1}+\cdots+c_{m}z_{m} , with c 1 , … , c n ∈ ℚ c_{1},\ldots,c_{n}\in\mathbb{Q} and z 1 , … , z n ∈ X ∪ B z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}\in X\cup B , and T T is a system of ILP constraints over X X and B B . An optimal solution of ( f , T ) (f,T) is a solution μ \mu of T T that maximizes f f among all solutions of T T , i.e., for every μ ′ ∈ 𝗌𝗈𝗅 ⁡ ( T ) \mu^{\prime}\in\mathsf{sol}(T) , it holds that μ ⁡ ( f ) = c 1 ​ μ ​ ( z 1 ) + ⋯ + c m ​ μ ​ ( z m ) ≥ μ ′ ​ ( f ) = c 1 ​ μ ′ ​ ( z 1 ) + ⋯ + c m ​ μ ′ ​ ( z m ) \mu(f)=c_{1}\mu(z_{1})+\cdots+c_{m}\mu(z_{m})\geq\mu^{\prime}(f)=c_{1}\mu^{\prime}(z_{1})+\cdots+c_{m}\mu^{\prime}(z_{m}) . We write 𝗈𝗉𝗍 ⁡ ( f , T ) \mathsf{opt}(f,T) for the set of all optimal solutions of ( f , T ) (f,T) . XOR and Indicator Constraints. For the sake of technical clarity, apart from linear constraints as defined above, we are also going to use xor constraints and indicator constraints, which we introduce below. It is well-known that xor and indicator constraints can be easily defined by means of linear constraints. Hence, in our technical development, we will directly use xor and indicator constraints to simplify the presentation, and we will refer to linear, xor, and indicator constraints simply as constraints. An xor constraint over B B is an expression of the form x ⊕ y = z , x\oplus y\ =\ z, where x , y , z x,y,z are binary variables from B B and ⊕ \oplus denotes the xor operator. An assignment μ \mu for B B satisfies the above xor constraint if μ ⁡ ( x ) ⊕ μ ⁡ ( y ) = μ ⁡ ( z ) \mu(x)\oplus\mu(y)=\mu(z) . Now, an indicator constraint over X X and B B is an expression of the form z ≡ a 1 x 1 + ⋯ a n x n ⋄ a 0 , z\ \equiv\ a_{1}x_{1}+\cdots a_{n}x_{n}\diamond a_{0}, where z ∈ B z\in B and a 1 x 1 + ⋯ a n x n ⋄ a 0 a_{1}x_{1}+\cdots a_{n}x_{n}\diamond a_{0} is a linear constraint over X X and B B . An assignment μ \mu for X X and B B satisfies the above indicator constraint when μ ⁡ ( z ) = 1 \mu(z)=1 iff μ \mu satisfies the linear constraint.

sections.heading: 5.2. Diverse Why-Provenance as an ILP Maximization Problem
sections.text: Having the basics of ILP in place, we can now introduce the general framework for casting ⋆ - ​ 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \star\text{-}\mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} , where ⋆ ∈ { 𝖠𝖫𝖫 , 𝖴𝖭 } \star\in\{\mathsf{ALL},\mathsf{UN}\} , as an ILP maximization problem based on different ILP encodings in a uniform way. To this end, we first introduce the general notion of ILP encoding of why-provenance. Definition 5.1 ( ILP Encoding ). Consider a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , a database D = { α 1 , … , α n } D=\{\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{n}\} over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , for an integer n > 0 n>0 , and a tuple t ¯ ∈ 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \bar{t}\in\mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} . An ILP encoding of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) , where ⋆ ∈ { 𝖠𝖫𝖫 , 𝖴𝖭 } \star\in\{\mathsf{ALL},\mathsf{UN}\} , is a system T T of ILP constraints over a set of integer variables X X and a set of binary variables B B , where B B contains n n distinguished variables x α 1 , … , x α n x_{\alpha_{1}},\ldots,x_{\alpha_{n}} , called the database variables of T T , such that, for all databases D ′ D^{\prime} over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , the following statements are equivalent: (1) D ′ ∈ 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) D^{\prime}\in\mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) . (2) D ′ = { α i ∣ i ∈ [ n ] ​ and ​ μ ​ ( x α i ) = 1 } D^{\prime}=\{\alpha_{i}\mid i\in[n]\text{ and }\mu(x_{\alpha_{i}})=1\} for some μ ∈ 𝗌𝗈𝗅 ⁡ ( T ) \mu\in\mathsf{sol}(T) . Therefore, given a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , and a tuple t ¯ ∈ 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \bar{t}\in\mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} , if we are able to construct an ILP encoding T T of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) , then we can compute all the members of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) by computing the solutions of T T . We now proceed explain how to use an ILP encoding for why-provenance as defined above (Definition 5.1 ) to solve ⋆ - ​ 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \star\text{-}\mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} . Consider an ILP encoding T T of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) over X X and B B , with x α 1 , … , x α n x_{\alpha_{1}},\ldots,x_{\alpha_{n}} being the database variables of T T . For an assignment μ \mu for X X and B B , we denote by 𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( μ ) \mathsf{db}(\mu) the database induced by μ \mu , that is, the database { α i ∣ i ∈ [ n ] ​ and ​ μ ​ ( x α i ) = 1 } \{\alpha_{i}\mid i\in[n]\text{ and }\mu(x_{\alpha_{i}})=1\} . For an integer i > 0 i>0 , the i i -th copy of T T , denoted T ( i ) T^{(i)} , is the system of ILP constraints over X ( i ) = { x ( i ) ∣ x ∈ X } X^{(i)}=\{x^{(i)}\mid x\in X\} and B ( i ) = { x ( i ) ∣ x ∈ B } B^{(i)}=\{x^{(i)}\mid x\in B\} obtained from T T by replacing each integer and binary variable x x with x ( i ) x^{(i)} . We are now ready to define the ILP maximization problem that allows us to solve ⋆ - ​ 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \star\text{-}\mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} . Definition 5.2 ( Maximization Problem ). Consider a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , a tuple t ¯ ∈ 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \bar{t}\in\mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} , and an integer k > 0 k>0 . Let T T be an ILP encoding of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) , for ⋆ ∈ { 𝖠𝖫𝖫 , 𝖴𝖭 } \star\in\{\mathsf{ALL},\mathsf{UN}\} , over X X and B B , with x α 1 , … , x α n x_{\alpha_{1}},\ldots,x_{\alpha_{n}} being the database variables of T T . The ( T , k ) (T,k) -problem is the ILP maximization problem ( f , S ) (f,S) over ⋃ i ∈ [ k ] X ( i ) \bigcup_{i\in[k]}X^{(i)} and ⋃ i ∈ [ k ] B ( i ) ∪ { 𝖺𝗎𝗑 ℓ i , j ∣ 1 ≤ ℓ ≤ n ​ and ​ 1 ≤ i < j ≤ k } \bigcup_{i\in[k]}B^{(i)}\cup\{\mathsf{aux}^{i,j}_{\ell}\mid 1\leq\ell\leq n\text{ and }1\leq i<j\leq k\} , where f f is defined as the expression ∑ 1 ≤ i < j ≤ k ( ∑ 1 ≤ ℓ ≤ n 𝖺𝗎𝗑 ℓ i , j ) , \sum\limits_{1\leq i<j\leq k}\left(\sum\limits_{1\leq\ell\leq n}\mathsf{aux}^{i,j}_{\ell}\right), and S S is the system of constraints T ( 1 ) ∪ ⋯ ∪ T ( k ) ∪ { x α ℓ ( i ) ⊕ x α ℓ ( j ) = 𝖺𝗎𝗑 ℓ i , j ∣ 1 ≤ ℓ ≤ n ​ and ​ 1 ≤ i < j ≤ k } ∪ { ∑ 1 ≤ ℓ ≤ n 𝖺𝗎𝗑 ℓ i , j ≥ 1 ∣ 1 ≤ i < j ≤ k } . T^{(1)}\cup\cdots\cup T^{(k)}\ \cup\\ \left\{x_{\alpha_{\ell}}^{(i)}\oplus x_{\alpha_{\ell}}^{(j)}=\mathsf{aux}^{i,j}_{\ell}\mid 1\leq\ell\leq n\text{ and }1\leq i<j\leq k\right\}\ \cup\\ \left\{\sum\limits_{1\leq\ell\leq n}\mathsf{aux}^{i,j}_{\ell}\geq 1\mid 1\leq i<j\leq k\right\}. Intuitively, the ( T , k ) (T,k) -problem defined above is a maximization problem which enforces the simultaneous satisfaction of k k distinct copies T ( 1 ) , … , T ( k ) T^{(1)},\ldots,T^{(k)} of T T . This makes a solution μ \mu of S S to be of the form μ 1 ∪ ⋯ ∪ μ k ∪ μ ′ \mu_{1}\cup\cdots\cup\mu_{k}\cup\mu^{\prime} , where μ ′ \mu^{\prime} is over the auxiliary variables, while each μ i \mu_{i} is a solution of T ( i ) T^{(i)} . In addition, S S forces μ 1 , … , μ k \mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{k} to induce pairwise different databases. The latter is guaranteed by the combination of the xor constraints and the additional linear constraints, apart from those of T ( 1 ) , … , T ( k ) T^{(1)},\ldots,T^{(k)} , added to S S . Hence, whenever S S is feasible, each solution of S S induces k k different members D 1 , … , D k D_{1},\ldots,D_{k} of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) . The expression f f is then used to maximize the diversity of the set { D 1 , … , D k } \{D_{1},\ldots,D_{k}\} where, for each i , j ∈ [ k ] i,j\in[k] with i < j i<j , the inner sum of f f encodes the distance between D i D_{i} and D j D_{j} . The above discussion is formalized by the following result. Theorem 5.3. Consider a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , a tuple t ¯ ∈ 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \bar{t}\in\mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} , and an integer k > 0 k>0 . Let T T be an ILP encoding of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) , for ⋆ ∈ { 𝖠𝖫𝖫 , 𝖴𝖭 } \star\in\{\mathsf{ALL},\mathsf{UN}\} , over X X and B B , with x α 1 , … , x α n x_{\alpha_{1}},\ldots,x_{\alpha_{n}} being the database variables of T T . For every set { D 1 , … , D k } \{D_{1},\ldots,D_{k}\} of databases over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , the following are equivalent: (1) { D 1 , … , D k } ∈ arg ​ max 𝒮 ∈ 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ k ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) ⁡ δ ​ ( 𝒮 ) \{D_{1},\ldots,D_{k}\}\in\argmax\limits_{\mathcal{S}\in\mathsf{why}_{\star}^{k}(\bar{t},D,Q)}\delta(\mathcal{S}) . (2) There is an optimal solution μ \mu of the ( T , k ) (T,k) -problem such that, for each i ∈ [ k ] i\in[k] , D i = { α ℓ ∣ ℓ ∈ [ n ] ​ and ​ μ ​ ( x α ℓ ( i ) ) = 1 } D_{i}=\{\alpha_{\ell}\mid\ell\in[n]\text{ and }\mu(x_{\alpha_{\ell}}^{(i)})=1\} . Observe now that Theorem 5.3 immediately leads to a procedure for solving ⋆ - ​ 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \star\text{-}\mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} , for ⋆ ∈ { 𝖠𝖫𝖫 , 𝖴𝖭 } \star\in\{\mathsf{ALL},\mathsf{UN}\} . In particular, assuming that 𝖡𝗎𝗂𝗅𝖽𝖨𝖫𝖯𝖤𝗇𝖼 \mathsf{BuildILPEnc} is a procedure that takes as input a triple ( t ¯ , D , Q ) (\bar{t},D,Q) , where Q Q is a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , D D is a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , and t ¯ \bar{t} a tuple of 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} , and constructs an ILP encoding for 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) , we define the procedure 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ 𝖡𝗎𝗂𝗅𝖽𝖨𝖫𝖯𝖤𝗇𝖼 ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{BuildILPEnc}] , which is depicted in Algorithm 1 , that solves ⋆ - ​ 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \star\text{-}\mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} . The correctness of the algorithm follows immediately from Theorem 5.3 and the fact that 𝖡𝗎𝗂𝗅𝖽𝖨𝖫𝖯𝖤𝗇𝖼 ⁡ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{BuildILPEnc}(\bar{t},D,Q) is an ILP encoding for 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) : Corollary 5.4. Let ⋆ ∈ { 𝖠𝖫𝖫 , 𝖴𝖭 } \star\in\{\mathsf{ALL},\mathsf{UN}\} , and assume that 𝖡𝗎𝗂𝗅𝖽𝖨𝖫𝖯𝖤𝗇𝖼 \mathsf{BuildILPEnc} is a procedure that takes as input a triple ( t ¯ , D , Q ) (\bar{t},D,Q) , where Q Q is a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , D D is a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , and t ¯ \bar{t} a tuple of 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} , and constructs an ILP encoding for 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) . Then, 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ 𝖡𝗎𝗂𝗅𝖽𝖨𝖫𝖯𝖤𝗇𝖼 ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{BuildILPEnc}] solves ⋆ - ​ 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \star\text{-}\mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} . Algorithm 1 Algorithm 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ 𝖡𝗎𝗂𝗅𝖽𝖨𝖫𝖯𝖤𝗇𝖼 ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{BuildILPEnc}] Input: A Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , a database D = { α 1 , … , α n } D=\{\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{n}\} over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , a tuple t ¯ ∈ 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \bar{t}\in\mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} , and an integer k > 0 k>0 . Output: A set consisting of k k databases, or fail . 1 T := 𝖡𝗎𝗂𝗅𝖽𝖨𝖫𝖯𝖤𝗇𝖼 ⁡ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) T:=\mathsf{BuildILPEnc}(\bar{t},D,Q) ; 2 Construct the ( T , k ) (T,k) -problem ( f , S ) (f,S) ; 3 if an optimal solution μ \mu of ( f , S ) (f,S) exists then 4 Let x α 1 , … , x α n x_{\alpha_{1}},\ldots,x_{\alpha_{n}} be the database variables of T T ; 5 for i = 1 i=1 to k k do 6 D i := { α ℓ ∣ ℓ ∈ [ n ] ​ and ​ μ ​ ( x α ℓ ( i ) ) = 1 } D_{i}:=\{\alpha_{\ell}\mid\ell\in[n]\text{ and }\mu(x_{\alpha_{\ell}}^{(i)})=1\} ; 7 return { D 1 , … , D k } \{D_{1},\ldots,D_{k}\} ; 8 else 9 return fail ;

sections.heading: 6. ILP Encodings of Why-Provenance
sections.text: We have seen that we can compute a solution of the problem ⋆ - ​ 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \star\text{-}\mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} , where ⋆ ∈ { 𝖠𝖫𝖫 , 𝖴𝖭 } \star\in\{\mathsf{ALL},\mathsf{UN}\} , on input Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , D D , t ¯ \bar{t} , and k > 0 k>0 , by simply finding an optimal solution of the ( T , k ) (T,k) -problem, where T T is any ILP encoding of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) . Moreover, 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ 𝖡𝗎𝗂𝗅𝖽𝖨𝖫𝖯𝖤𝗇𝖼 ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{BuildILPEnc}] is a procedure that precisely does that, given that the sub-procedure 𝖡𝗎𝗂𝗅𝖽𝖨𝖫𝖯𝖤𝗇𝖼 \mathsf{BuildILPEnc} is able to construct the ILP encoding T T . In this section, we describe concrete ILP encodings of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) , which will lead to concrete means to implement the sub-procedure 𝖡𝗎𝗂𝗅𝖽𝖨𝖫𝖯𝖤𝗇𝖼 \mathsf{BuildILPEnc} . To this end, we present the main characterizations from the literature of when a database D ′ ⊆ D D^{\prime}\subseteq D is a member of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) , or equivalently, when there is an arbitrary (resp., unambiguous) proof tree T T of the fact R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) R(\bar{t}) w.r.t. D D and Σ \Sigma with 𝗌𝗎𝗉𝗉𝗈𝗋𝗍 ⁡ ( T ) = D ′ \mathsf{support}(T)=D^{\prime} . For each such characterization, we discuss how it can be used to devise ILP encodings of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) . Before we proceed further, we need to discuss some basic assumptions and recall some auxiliary notions. Programs. In order to simplify the technical definitions, in the rest of this section, for a Datalog program Σ \Sigma , we assume that for each rule σ ∈ Σ \sigma\in\Sigma of the form R 0 ( x ¯ 0 ) :– R 1 ( x ¯ 1 ) , … , R n ( x ¯ n ) R_{0}(\bar{x}_{0})\ \text{:--}\ R_{1}(\bar{x}_{1}),\ldots,R_{n}(\bar{x}_{n}) , the predicates R 1 , … , R n R_{1},\ldots,R_{n} are all distinct, i.e., rule-bodies are self-join-free. The latter assumption can be done w.l.o.g. since we can always convert Σ \Sigma into Σ ′ \Sigma^{\prime} that satisfies the desired condition without affecting the why-provenance of R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) R(\bar{t}) w.r.t. D D and Σ \Sigma relative to both arbitrary and unambiguous proof trees. In particular, for each rule σ \sigma as above, and for each i ∈ [ n ] i\in[n] , let Aux i σ ∉ 𝗌𝖼𝗁 ⁡ ( Σ ) \text{\rm Aux}^{\sigma}_{i}\not\in\mathsf{sch}(\Sigma) be an auxiliary predicate of arity 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R i ) \mathsf{ar}(R_{i}) , replace R i R_{i} with Aux i σ \text{\rm Aux}^{\sigma}_{i} in the body of σ \sigma , and add to Σ \Sigma the rule Aux i σ ( x 1 , … , x 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R i ) ) :– R i ( x 1 , … , x 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R i ) ) \text{\rm Aux}^{\sigma}_{i}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{\mathsf{ar}(R_{i})})\ \text{:--}\ R_{i}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{\mathsf{ar}(R_{i})}) . Clearly, for ⋆ ∈ { 𝖠𝖫𝖫 , 𝖴𝖭 } \star\in\{\mathsf{ALL},\mathsf{UN}\} , 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) = 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ′ ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q)=\mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q^{\prime}) , where Q ′ = ( Σ ′ , R ) Q^{\prime}=(\Sigma^{\prime},R) . Multisets. A multiset M M is a pair ( S , μ ) (S,\mu) , where S S is a set and μ : S → ℕ \mu:S\rightarrow\mathbb{N} is a function assigning to each element a ∈ S a\in S a strictly positive integer, called the multiplicity of a a in S S . We say that M M is empty if S S is empty; otherwise, it is non-empty. The cardinality of M M , denoted | M | |M| , is ∑ a ∈ S μ ⁡ ( a ) \sum\limits_{a\in S}\mu(a) . By abuse of notation, we may write a ∈ M a\in M meaning that a ∈ S a\in S . Moreover, we may write | M ⁡ ( a ) | |M(a)| for μ ⁡ ( a ) \mu(a) , if a ∈ S a\in S , and 0 0 if a ∉ S a\not\in S . Finally, for a sequence of (not necessarily distinct) objects o 1 , … , o n o_{1},\ldots,o_{n} , we write { { o 1 , … , o n } } \{\!\{o_{1},\ldots,o_{n}\}\!\} to denote the multiset ( S , μ ) (S,\mu) , where S = { o 1 , … , o n } S=\{o_{1},\ldots,o_{n}\} and μ \mu assigns to each element of S S the number of times the element occurs in the sequence o 1 , … , o n o_{1},\ldots,o_{n} . Downward Closure. We now introduce the so-called downward closure of a fact w.r.t. a database and a Datalog program, taken from ( Elhalawati et al., 2022 ) , that will play a key role in all the characterizations we are going to discuss. Roughly, the downward closure of a fact α \alpha w.r.t. a database D D and a Datalog program Σ \Sigma is a hypergraph that encodes all possible proof trees of α \alpha w.r.t. D D and Σ \Sigma . For our purposes, a (directed) hypergraph ℋ \mathcal{H} is a pair ( V , E ) (V,E) , where V V is the set of its nodes and E E is the set of its hyperedges , i.e., pairs of the form ( u , T ) (u,T) , where u ∈ V u\in V and T ⊆ V T\subseteq V is a non-empty set of nodes. For u , v ∈ V u,v\in V , we say that u u reaches v v in ℋ \mathcal{H} if either u = v u=v , or there exists a sequence of hyperedges ( u 1 , T 1 ) , … , ( u n , T n ) (u_{1},T_{1}),\ldots,(u_{n},T_{n}) with u 1 = u u_{1}=u , v ∈ T n v\in T_{n} , and u i ∈ T i − 1 u_{i}\in T_{i-1} for each i ∈ { 2 , … , n } i\in\{2,\ldots,n\} . For a node u u , we write ℋ ↓ u \mathcal{H}_{\downarrow u} for the hypergraph ( V ′ , E ′ ) (V^{\prime},E^{\prime}) obtained from ℋ \mathcal{H} , where V ′ V^{\prime} contains u u and all nodes reachable from u u , and E ′ E^{\prime} collects all the hyperedges mentioning only nodes of V ′ V^{\prime} . For a Datalog program Σ \Sigma and a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , the graph of rule instances (GRI) of D D and Σ \Sigma is the hypergraph 𝗀𝗋𝗂 ⁡ ( D , Σ ) = ( V , E ) \mathsf{gri}(D,\Sigma)=(V,E) , with V ⊆ 𝖻𝖺𝗌𝖾 ⁡ ( D , Σ ) V\subseteq\mathsf{base}(D,\Sigma) , such that (1) D ⊆ V D\subseteq V , and (2) if there exists a rule R 0 ( x ¯ 0 ) :– R 1 ( x ¯ 1 ) , … , R n ( x ¯ n ) R_{0}(\bar{x}_{0})\ \text{:--}\ R_{1}(\bar{x}_{1}),\ldots,R_{n}(\bar{x}_{n}) in Σ \Sigma and a function h : ⋃ i ∈ [ n ] x ¯ i → 𝐂 h:\bigcup_{i\in[n]}\bar{x}_{i}\rightarrow\mathbf{C} such that α i = R i ​ ( h ⁡ ( x ¯ i ) ) ∈ V \alpha_{i}=R_{i}(h(\bar{x}_{i}))\in V , for i ∈ [ n ] i\in[n] , then α 0 = R 0 ​ ( h ⁡ ( x ¯ 0 ) ) ∈ V \alpha_{0}=R_{0}(h(\bar{x}_{0}))\in V and ( α 0 , { α 1 , … , α n } ) (\alpha_{0},\{\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{n}\}) is an hyperedge of E E . Intuitively, 𝗀𝗋𝗂 ⁡ ( D , Σ ) \mathsf{gri}(D,\Sigma) encodes all the proof trees of some fact α \alpha w.r.t. D D and Σ \Sigma . Since we are interested only in the proof trees of a specific fact α \alpha , we do not need to consider 𝗀𝗋𝗂 ⁡ ( D , Σ ) \mathsf{gri}(D,\Sigma) in its entirety, but only the subhypergraph of 𝗀𝗋𝗂 ⁡ ( D , Σ ) \mathsf{gri}(D,\Sigma) containing α \alpha and all the nodes reachable from it. This leads to the notion of downward closure, which simply keeps from 𝗀𝗋𝗂 ⁡ ( D , Σ ) \mathsf{gri}(D,\Sigma) the part that is relevant to derive the fact in question. Definition 6.1 ( Downward Closure ). Consider a Datalog program Σ \Sigma , a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , and a fact α \alpha occurring in 𝗀𝗋𝗂 ⁡ ( D , Σ ) \mathsf{gri}(D,\Sigma) . The downward closure of α \alpha w.r.t. D D and Σ \Sigma , denoted 𝖽𝗈𝗐𝗇 ⁡ ( α , D , Σ ) \mathsf{down}(\alpha,D,\Sigma) , is the hypergraph 𝗀𝗋𝗂 ​ ( D , Σ ) ↓ α \mathsf{gri}(D,\Sigma)_{\downarrow\alpha} . In the rest of the section, whenever we refer to an ILP encoding of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) , for a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , and a tuple t ¯ ∈ 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \bar{t}\in\mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} , we tacitly assume that R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) R(\bar{t}) occurs in 𝗀𝗋𝗂 ⁡ ( D , Σ ) \mathsf{gri}(D,\Sigma) , or, equivalently, that t ¯ ∈ Q ⁡ ( D ) \bar{t}\in Q(D) , so that the hypergraph 𝖽𝗈𝗐𝗇 ⁡ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , D , Σ ) \mathsf{down}(R(\bar{t}),D,\Sigma) is well-defined. This is w.l.o.g. since, if R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) R(\bar{t}) does not occur in 𝗀𝗋𝗂 ⁡ ( D , Σ ) \mathsf{gri}(D,\Sigma) , then 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) = ∅ \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q)=\emptyset , and thus the unfeasible system consisting of the two constraints v ≥ 1 v\geq 1 and v ≤ 0 v\leq 0 , where v v is one of the database variables, is trivially an ILP encoding of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) . We are now ready to present the ILP encodings of interest. Those encodings are classified into two main categories, namely the hypergaph- and the graph-based ones, depending on whether the underlying characterization of when a database is a member of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) , for ⋆ ∈ { 𝖠𝖫𝖫 , 𝖴𝖭 } \star\in\{\mathsf{ALL},\mathsf{UN}\} , uses a hypergraph or a (directed acyclic) graph as a way for compactly representing proof trees.

sections.heading: 6.1. Hypergraph-based ILP Encodings
sections.text: We start by recalling the characterizations of interest that rely on hypergraphs, and then use them to devise the hypergraph-based ILP encodings of why-provenance. Hypergraph-based Characterizations Consider a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , and a tuple t ¯ ∈ 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \bar{t}\in\mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} . For a multiset E = ( E ′ , μ ) E=(E^{\prime},\mu) of hyperedges from 𝖽𝗈𝗐𝗇 ⁡ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , D , Σ ) \mathsf{down}(R(\bar{t}),D,\Sigma) , we denote by V E V_{E} the set of nodes occurring in the hyperedges of E E and by ℋ E \mathcal{H}_{E} the hypergraph ( V E , E ′ ) (V_{E},E^{\prime}) . For a node α ∈ V E \alpha\in V_{E} , we define the in-degree of α \alpha in E E , denoted 𝗂𝗇 E ​ ( α ) \mathsf{in}_{E}(\alpha) , as the number of (possibly repeated) hyperedges of E E in which α \alpha appears as a target, namely 𝗂𝗇 E ​ ( α ) = ∑ ( β , T ) ∈ E ′ ​ with ​ α ∈ T μ ⁡ ( ( β , T ) ) . \mathsf{in}_{E}(\alpha)=\sum\limits_{(\beta,T)\in E^{\prime}\text{ with }\alpha\in T}\mu((\beta,T)). Moreover, the out-degree of α \alpha in E E , denoted 𝗈𝗎𝗍 E ​ ( α ) \mathsf{out}_{E}(\alpha) , is the number of (possibly repeated) hyperedges in E E having α \alpha as the source, i.e., 𝗈𝗎𝗍 E ​ ( α ) = ∑ ( α , T ) ∈ E ′ μ ⁡ ( ( α , T ) ) . \mathsf{out}_{E}(\alpha)=\sum\limits_{(\alpha,T)\in E^{\prime}}\mu((\alpha,T)). We are now ready to recall the hypergraph-based characterization of when there is a proof tree of R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) R(\bar{t}) w.r.t. D D and Σ \Sigma with a certain support D ′ ⊆ D D^{\prime}\subseteq D . This relies on the existence of a multiset of hyperedges with certain properties that one can extract from 𝖽𝗈𝗐𝗇 ⁡ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , D , Σ ) \mathsf{down}(R(\bar{t}),D,\Sigma) . We proceed to introduce those properties. Definition 6.2 ( (Unambiguous) Proof Tree Description ). Consider a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , a tuple t ¯ ∈ 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \bar{t}\in\mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} , and a database D ′ ⊆ D D^{\prime}\subseteq D . We say that a multiset E E of hyperedges from 𝖽𝗈𝗐𝗇 ⁡ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , D , Σ ) \mathsf{down}(R(\bar{t}),D,\Sigma) is a description of a proof tree of R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) R(\bar{t}) w.r.t. D D and Σ \Sigma with support D ′ D^{\prime} if the following hold: (1) R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) ∈ V E R(\bar{t})\in V_{E} and 𝗈𝗎𝗍 E ​ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) ) − 𝗂𝗇 E ​ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) ) = 1 \mathsf{out}_{E}(R(\bar{t}))-\mathsf{in}_{E}(R(\bar{t}))=1 , (2) 𝗈𝗎𝗍 E ​ ( α ) − 𝗂𝗇 E ​ ( α ) = 0 \mathsf{out}_{E}(\alpha)-\mathsf{in}_{E}(\alpha)=0 , for each α ∈ V E ∖ ( D ∪ { R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) } ) \alpha\in V_{E}\setminus(D\cup\{R(\bar{t})\}) , (3) ∑ α ∈ V E ∩ D 𝗂𝗇 E ​ ( α ) ≥ 1 \sum\limits_{\alpha\in V_{E}\cap D}\mathsf{in}_{E}(\alpha)\geq 1 , (4) R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) R(\bar{t}) reaches all nodes of ℋ E \mathcal{H}_{E} in ℋ E \mathcal{H}_{E} , and (5) D ′ = V E ∩ D D^{\prime}=V_{E}\cap D . We say that E E is a description of an unambiguous proof tree of R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) R(\bar{t}) w.r.t. D D and Σ \Sigma with support D ′ D^{\prime} if, in addition to the above conditions, for every pair ( α , T ) , ( α , T ′ ) ∈ E (\alpha,T),(\alpha,T^{\prime})\in E , it holds that T = T ′ T=T^{\prime} . The desired hypergraph-based characterizations follows: Theorem 6.3 ( ( Calautti et al., 2024a ) ). Consider a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , a tuple t ¯ ∈ 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \bar{t}\in\mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} , and a database D ′ ⊆ D D^{\prime}\subseteq D . The following are equivalent: (1) There is a proof tree (resp., an unambiguous proof tree) of R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) R(\bar{t}) w.r.t. D D and Σ \Sigma with support D ′ D^{\prime} . (2) There is a description E E of a proof tree (resp., an unambiguous proof tree) of R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) R(\bar{t}) w.r.t. D D and Σ \Sigma with support D ′ D^{\prime} . Note that the version of Theorem 6.3 for unambiguous proof trees has not been explicitly stated in ( Calautti et al., 2024a ) , but it is an easy adaptation of its version for arbitrary proof trees. We now show how to exploit Theorem 6.3 to devise an ILP encoding of why-provenance. Hypergraph-based ILP Encoding In what follows, fix a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , a tuple t ¯ ∈ 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \bar{t}\in\mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} , and let 𝖽𝗈𝗐𝗇 ⁡ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , D , Σ ) = ( V , E ) \mathsf{down}(R(\bar{t}),D,\Sigma)=(V,E) . We start with the ILP encoding for 𝗐𝗁𝗒 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) , called the hypergraph-based ILP encoding of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) and denoted as 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) . The high-level idea is to devise a set of constraints whose solutions correspond to descriptions of proof trees of R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) R(\bar{t}) w.r.t. D D and Σ \Sigma with some support D ′ D^{\prime} . This will imply that from each solution of 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) one can extract the support D ′ D^{\prime} of a proof tree of R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) R(\bar{t}) w.r.t. D D and Σ \Sigma , and thus 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) would indeed be an ILP encoding for 𝗐𝗁𝗒 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) . Formally, 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) is a system of constraints over integer variables X X and binary variables B B as follows. The Variables of 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) . For each hyperedge ( α , T ) (\alpha,T) of 𝖽𝗈𝗐𝗇 ⁡ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , D , Σ ) \mathsf{down}(R(\bar{t}),D,\Sigma) , the set X X contains one integer variable x ( α , T ) x_{(\alpha,T)} . Intuitively, the value of x ( α , T ) x_{(\alpha,T)} in a solution of 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) denotes the multiplicity of ( α , T ) (\alpha,T) in the underlying multiset that is a description of a proof tree of R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) R(\bar{t}) w.r.t. D D and Σ \Sigma with some support D ′ D^{\prime} . Let us denote this multiset as E ∗ E^{*} . In particular, when x ( α , T ) x_{(\alpha,T)} is 0 0 , it means that the hyperedge is not part of E ∗ E^{*} . Moreover, assuming E ^ \hat{E} denotes the set of (standard) edges induced by the hyperedges of 𝖽𝗈𝗐𝗇 ⁡ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , D , Σ ) \mathsf{down}(R(\bar{t}),D,\Sigma) , i.e., E ^ = { ( α , β ) ∣ ( α , { … , β , … } ) ∈ E } \hat{E}=\{(\alpha,\beta)\mid(\alpha,\{\ldots,\beta,\ldots\})\in E\} , X X contains an integer variable y ( α , β ) y_{(\alpha,\beta)} , for each edge ( α , β ) ∈ E ^ (\alpha,\beta)\in\hat{E} . Such variables will be used in some constraints of 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) to guarantee that R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) R(\bar{t}) reaches all nodes of ℋ E ∗ \mathcal{H}_{E^{*}} , and they encode the amount of "flow" going through these edges; more details on this later. Finally, B B contains one binary variable z α z_{\alpha} for each α ∈ V ∪ D \alpha\in V\cup D . The Constraints of 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) . We now move to the constraints. The system 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) is a set of constraints T 𝖽𝖾𝗀𝗋𝖾𝖾 ∪ T 𝗋𝖾𝖺𝖼𝗁 ∪ T 𝖻𝗂𝗇𝖽 ∪ T 𝗉𝗈𝗌 . T_{\mathsf{degree}}\cup T_{\mathsf{reach}}\cup T_{\mathsf{bind}}\cup T_{\mathsf{pos}}. The constraints of T 𝖽𝖾𝗀𝗋𝖾𝖾 T_{\mathsf{degree}} force the in- and out-degree of the nodes of the multiset E ∗ E^{*} to enjoy the properties (1)-(3) of Definition 6.2 . The constraints T 𝗋𝖾𝖺𝖼𝗁 T_{\mathsf{reach}} enforce property (4) of Definition 6.2 , i.e., that R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) R(\bar{t}) reaches all nodes of ℋ E ∗ \mathcal{H}_{E^{*}} ; the latter exploits the variables of the form y ( α , β ) y_{(\alpha,\beta)} discussed above. Finally, the constraints of T 𝖻𝗂𝗇𝖽 T_{\mathsf{bind}} simply force each binary variable z α z_{\alpha} with α ∈ V \alpha\in V to be true iff at least one hyperedge mentioning α \alpha belongs to E ∗ E^{*} , and in case α ∉ V \alpha\not\in V , i.e., α ∈ D ∖ V \alpha\in D\setminus V , force z α z_{\alpha} to be always false; this is needed to enforce property (5) of Definition 6.2 , guaranteeing that only database facts occurring in V V can form a member of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) . 1 1 1 Note that we do not refer to any specific set D ′ D^{\prime} of facts when implementing property (5) of Definition 6.2 . This is because we want the solutions of our system to induce all possible members of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) , rather than a specific database D ′ D^{\prime} . Finally, the constraints of T 𝗉𝗈𝗌 T_{\mathsf{pos}} state that the integer variables, which are meant to represent multiplicities and flows, take non-negative values. We proceed to formalize the above informal description. For each node α ∈ V \alpha\in V of 𝖽𝗈𝗐𝗇 ⁡ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , D , Σ ) \mathsf{down}(R(\bar{t}),D,\Sigma) , let ℐ α = ∑ ( β , T ) ∈ E ​ with ​ α ∈ T x ( β , T ) and 𝒪 α = ∑ ( α , T ) ∈ E x ( α , T ) . \mathcal{I}_{\alpha}=\sum\limits_{(\beta,T)\in E\text{ with }\alpha\in T}x_{(\beta,T)}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathcal{O}_{\alpha}=\sum\limits_{(\alpha,T)\in E}x_{(\alpha,T)}. The expressions ℐ α \mathcal{I}_{\alpha} and 𝒪 α \mathcal{O}_{\alpha} essentially compute the integers 𝗂𝗇 E ∗ ​ ( α ) \mathsf{in}_{E^{*}}(\alpha) and 𝗈𝗎𝗍 E ∗ ​ ( α ) \mathsf{out}_{E^{*}}(\alpha) , respectively. With those expressions in place, T 𝖽𝖾𝗀𝗋𝖾𝖾 T_{\mathsf{degree}} and T 𝖻𝗂𝗇𝖽 T_{\mathsf{bind}} are easily defined. In particular, T 𝖽𝖾𝗀𝗋𝖾𝖾 T_{\mathsf{degree}} is the set { 𝒪 R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) − ℐ R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) = 1 } \displaystyle\left\{\mathcal{O}_{R(\bar{t})}-\mathcal{I}_{R(\bar{t})}=1\right\} ∪ \displaystyle\cup { 𝒪 α − ℐ α = 0 ∣ α ∈ V ∖ ( D ∪ { R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) } ) } \displaystyle\left\{\mathcal{O}_{\alpha}-\mathcal{I}_{\alpha}=0\mid\alpha\in V\setminus(D\cup\{R(\bar{t})\})\right\} ∪ \displaystyle\cup { ∑ α ∈ V ∩ D ℐ α ≥ 1 } , \displaystyle\left\{\sum\limits_{\alpha\in V\cap D}\mathcal{I}_{\alpha}\geq 1\right\}, and T 𝖻𝗂𝗇𝖽 T_{\mathsf{bind}} is the set of constraints { z α ≡ ℐ α + 𝒪 α ≥ 1 ∣ α ∈ V } ∪ { z α = 0 ∣ α ∈ D ∖ V } . \left\{z_{\alpha}\equiv\mathcal{I}_{\alpha}+\mathcal{O}_{\alpha}\geq 1\mid\alpha\in V\right\}\cup\left\{z_{\alpha}=0\mid\alpha\in D\setminus V\right\}. Finally, T 𝗉𝗈𝗌 T_{\mathsf{pos}} is the set of constraints { x ( α , T ) ≥ 0 ∣ ( α , T ) ∈ E } ∪ { y ( α , β ) ≥ 0 ∣ ( α , β ) ∈ E ^ } . \left\{x_{(\alpha,T)}\geq 0\mid(\alpha,T)\in E\right\}\cup\left\{y_{(\alpha,\beta)}\geq 0\mid(\alpha,\beta)\in\hat{E}\right\}. It remains to explain how the set T 𝗋𝖾𝖺𝖼𝗁 T_{\mathsf{reach}} is defined. For this, we exploit the variables of the form y ( α , β ) y_{(\alpha,\beta)} , for each ( α , β ) ∈ E ^ (\alpha,\beta)\in\hat{E} . Intuitively, each variable y ( α , β ) y_{(\alpha,\beta)} denotes the amount of “flow” the edge carries when traversing it. The constraints of T 𝗋𝖾𝖺𝖼𝗁 T_{\mathsf{reach}} will exploit these variables to solve the reachability problem on the (standard) directed graph induced by the hyperedges of E ∗ E^{*} . We do this using a flow-based encoding. Informally, T 𝗋𝖾𝖺𝖼𝗁 T_{\mathsf{reach}} will enforce three constraints (i) every edge ( α , β ) ∈ E ^ (\alpha,\beta)\in\hat{E} carries zero flow, unless some hyperedge of E ∗ E^{*} with source α \alpha mentions β \beta in its target, in which case it can carry an amount of flow that is enough to be distributed to all other nodes, (ii) the net outgoing flow of node R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) R(\bar{t}) , i.e., the difference between the total outgoing flow and the total incoming flow of R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) R(\bar{t}) , is enough to be distributed evenly to all other nodes of E ∗ E^{*} , and (iii) for every other node α \alpha that appears in E ∗ E^{*} , the total outgoing flow of α \alpha must decrease by 1 w.r.t. the total incoming flow of α \alpha (this is to guarantee that α \alpha consumes precisely its share of the total flow). We now formalize the above intuitive discussion. For a node α ∈ V \alpha\in V , let ℱ α 𝗂𝗇 = ∑ ( β , α ) ∈ E ^ y ( β , α ) and ℱ α 𝗈𝗎𝗍 = ∑ ( α , β ) ∈ E ^ y ( α , β ) , \mathcal{F}^{\mathsf{in}}_{\alpha}=\sum\limits_{(\beta,\alpha)\in\hat{E}}y_{(\beta,\alpha)}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathcal{F}^{\mathsf{out}}_{\alpha}=\sum\limits_{(\alpha,\beta)\in\hat{E}}y_{(\alpha,\beta)}, referring the total incoming and outgoing flow of node α \alpha , respectively. Moreover, for an edge ( α , β ) ∈ E ^ (\alpha,\beta)\in\hat{E} , let 𝒞 ( α , β ) = ∑ ( α , T ) ∈ E ​ with ​ β ∈ T x ( α , T ) , \mathcal{C}_{(\alpha,\beta)}=\sum\limits_{(\alpha,T)\in E\text{ with }\beta\in T}x_{(\alpha,T)}, which counts, with multiplicities, the hyperedges of E ∗ E^{*} that have α \alpha as the source and mention β \beta in their target; hence, 𝒞 ( α , β ) \mathcal{C}_{(\alpha,\beta)} is greater than zero precisely when ( α , β ) (\alpha,\beta) is an edge of the directed graph induced by the hyperedges of E ∗ E^{*} .
