This completes the definition of 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) . We proceed to formally show that it is an ILP encoding of why-provenance: Theorem 6.4. Consider a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , a database D = { α 1 , … , α n } D=\{\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{n}\} over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , and a tuple t ¯ ∈ 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \bar{t}\in\mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} . The system of ILP constraints 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) is an ILP encoding of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) with database variables z α 1 , … , z α n z_{\alpha_{1}},\ldots,z_{\alpha_{n}} . By Theorem 6.4 and Corollary 5.4 , we obtain that: Corollary 6.5. 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}}] solves the problem 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ - ​ 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \mathsf{ALL}\text{-}\mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} . Unambiguous Hypergraph-based ILP Encoding In what follows, fix a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , a tuple t ¯ ∈ 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \bar{t}\in\mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} , and assume 𝖽𝗈𝗐𝗇 ⁡ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , D , Σ ) = ( V , E ) \mathsf{down}(R(\bar{t}),D,\Sigma)=(V,E) . We proceed to show how to construct the ILP encoding of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 𝖴𝖭 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\mathsf{UN}}(\bar{t},D,Q) . Recall that the unambiguous hypergraph-based characterization only requires one additional property compared to the hypergraph-based characterization. Hence, we can easily define the ILP encoding of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 𝖴𝖭 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\mathsf{UN}}(\bar{t},D,Q) , dubbed 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖴𝖭 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{UN}}(\bar{t},D,Q) , by simply adding the required constraints to 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) . Let X X and B B be the sets of integer and binary variables, respectively, of 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) . Now, the variables of 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖴𝖭 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{UN}}(\bar{t},D,Q) are X ∪ B ∪ B ′ X\cup B\cup B^{\prime} , where B ′ B^{\prime} is the set of binary variables { x ^ ( α , T ) ∣ ( α , T ) ∈ E } . \{\hat{x}_{(\alpha,T)}\mid(\alpha,T)\in E\}. Intuitively, in a solution of 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖴𝖭 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{UN}}(\bar{t},D,Q) , which induces a multiset E ∗ E^{*} of hyperedges of 𝖽𝗈𝗐𝗇 ⁡ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , D , Σ ) \mathsf{down}(R(\bar{t}),D,\Sigma) that is a description of an unambiguous proof tree of R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) R(\bar{t}) w.r.t. D D and Σ \Sigma with some support D ′ D^{\prime} , each variable x ^ ( α , T ) \hat{x}_{(\alpha,T)} is true iff the hyperedge ( α , T ) (\alpha,T) occurs in E ∗ E^{*} . Finally, 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖴𝖭 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{UN}}(\bar{t},D,Q) is defined as 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) ∪ T 𝖴𝖭 , \mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q)\cup T_{\mathsf{UN}}, where T 𝖴𝖭 T_{\mathsf{UN}} is the set of constraints enforcing the additional required condition, that is, no two hyperedges ( α , T ) , ( α , T ′ ) (\alpha,T),(\alpha,T^{\prime}) appear in E ∗ E^{*} with T ≠ T ′ T\neq T^{\prime} . This is achieved by defining T 𝖴𝖭 T_{\mathsf{UN}} as follows: { x ^ ( α , T ) ≡ x ( α , T ) ≥ 1 ∣ ( α , T ) ∈ E } ∪ { ∑ ( α , T ) ∈ E x ^ ( α , T ) ≤ 1 ∣ α ∈ V } . \left\{\hat{x}_{(\alpha,T)}\equiv x_{(\alpha,T)}\geq 1\mid(\alpha,T)\in E\right\}\cup\left\{\sum\limits_{(\alpha,T)\in E}\hat{x}_{(\alpha,T)}\leq 1\mid\alpha\in V\right\}. We can now formally show that 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖴𝖭 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{UN}}(\bar{t},D,Q) is indeed an ILP encoding of why-provenance: Theorem 6.6. Consider a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , a database D = { α 1 , … , α n } D=\{\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{n}\} over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , and a tuple t ¯ ∈ 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \bar{t}\in\mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} . The system of ILP constraints 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖴𝖭 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{UN}}(\bar{t},D,Q) is an ILP encoding of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 𝖴𝖭 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\mathsf{UN}}(\bar{t},D,Q) with database variables z α 1 , … , z α n z_{\alpha_{1}},\ldots,z_{\alpha_{n}} . By Theorem 6.6 and Corollary 5.4 , we obtain that: Corollary 6.7. 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖴𝖭 ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{UN}}] solves the problem 𝖴𝖭 ​ - ​ 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \mathsf{UN}\text{-}\mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} .

sections.heading: 6.2. Graph-based ILP Encodings
sections.text: We now recall the characterizations of when there exists an (unambiguous) proof tree of some fact R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) R(\bar{t}) w.r.t. some database D D and Datalog program Σ \Sigma with some support D ′ D^{\prime} that rely on the existence of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) with certain properties, called a proof DAG of R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) R(\bar{t}) w.r.t. D D and Σ \Sigma , and then use them to devise the graph-based ILP encodings of why-provenance. Graph-based Characterizations The characterizations of interest state that every (unambiguous) proof tree admits a corresponding (unambiguous) proof DAG G G , where for each fact α \alpha , only a “small” number of nodes of G G are labeled with α \alpha . In fact, in the case of arbitrary proof DAGs, this number is bounded by a certain polynomial that depends on some parameters of the downward closure of α \alpha w.r.t. D D and Σ \Sigma , whereas in the case of unambiguous proof DAGs, this number is 1 1 . We proceed to recall (unambiguous) proof DAGs and then present the actual characterizations. We recall that a DAG G G is rooted if it has exactly one node, the root , with no incoming edges. A node of G G is a leaf if it has no outgoing edges. Definition 6.8 ( (Unambiguous) Proof DAG ). Consider a Datalog program Σ \Sigma , a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , and a fact α \alpha over 𝗌𝖼𝗁 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{sch}(\Sigma) . A proof DAG of α \alpha w.r.t. D D and Σ \Sigma is a finite labeled rooted DAG G = ( V , E , λ ) G=(V,E,\lambda) , with λ : V → 𝖻𝖺𝗌𝖾 ⁡ ( D , Σ ) \lambda:V\rightarrow\mathsf{base}(D,\Sigma) , such that: (1) If v ∈ V v\in V is the root, then λ ⁡ ( v ) = α \lambda(v)=\alpha . (2) If v ∈ V v\in V is a leaf, then λ ⁡ ( v ) ∈ D \lambda(v)\in D . (3) If v ∈ V v\in V has n ≥ 1 n\geq 1 outgoing edges ( v , u 1 ) , … , ( v , u n ) (v,u_{1}),\ldots,(v,u_{n}) , then there exists a rule R 0 ( x ¯ 0 ) :– R 1 ( x ¯ 1 ) , … , R n ( x ¯ n ) ∈ Σ R_{0}(\bar{x}_{0})\ \text{:--}\ R_{1}(\bar{x}_{1}),\ldots,R_{n}(\bar{x}_{n})\in\Sigma and a function h : ⋃ i ∈ [ n ] x ¯ i → 𝐂 h:\bigcup_{i\in[n]}\bar{x}_{i}\rightarrow\mathbf{C} such that λ ⁡ ( v ) = R 0 ​ ( h ⁡ ( x ¯ 0 ) ) \lambda(v)=R_{0}(h(\bar{x}_{0})) , and λ ⁡ ( u i ) = R i ​ ( h ⁡ ( x ¯ i ) ) \lambda(u_{i})=R_{i}(h(\bar{x}_{i})) for each i ∈ [ n ] i\in[n] . We say that G G is an unambiguous proof DAG of α \alpha w.r.t. D D and Σ \Sigma if, in addition to the above conditions, for every two nodes u , v ∈ V u,v\in V , it holds that λ ⁡ ( u ) = λ ⁡ ( v ) \lambda(u)=\lambda(v) implies u = v u=v . The difference between a proof tree and a proof DAG is that a proof DAG might reuse nodes to compactly represent a proof tree. In fact, every proof tree is a proof DAG where each node has at most one parent. As for proof trees, given a proof DAG G G (of some fact w.r.t. some database and Datalog program), its support, denoted 𝗌𝗎𝗉𝗉𝗈𝗋𝗍 ⁡ ( G ) \mathsf{support}(G) , is the set of facts that label the leaves of G G . We can now recall the desired graph-based characterizations. In what follows, with 𝖽𝗈𝗐𝗇 ⁡ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , D , Σ ) = ( V , E ) \mathsf{down}(R(\bar{t}),D,\Sigma)=(V,E) , for some Datalog program Σ \Sigma , database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , and fact R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) R(\bar{t}) , let 𝖻𝗈𝗎𝗇𝖽 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , D , Σ ) \displaystyle\mathsf{bound}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(R(\bar{t}),D,\Sigma) = \displaystyle= ( | V | ⋅ d + 1 ) ⋅ d ⋅ b , \displaystyle(|V|\cdot d+1)\cdot d\cdot b, 𝖻𝗈𝗎𝗇𝖽 𝖴𝖭 ​ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , D , Σ ) \displaystyle\mathsf{bound}_{\mathsf{UN}}(R(\bar{t}),D,\Sigma) = \displaystyle= 1 , \displaystyle 1, where d = | V ∩ D | d=|V\cap D| , i.e., d d is the number of nodes of 𝖽𝗈𝗐𝗇 ⁡ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , D , Σ ) \mathsf{down}(R(\bar{t}),D,\Sigma) that correspond to database facts, and b = max ⁡ { | T | ∣ ( α , T ) ∈ E } b=\max\{|T|\mid(\alpha,T)\in E\} is the maximum “branching” of a hyperedge of 𝖽𝗈𝗐𝗇 ⁡ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , D , Σ ) \mathsf{down}(R(\bar{t}),D,\Sigma) . Theorem 6.9 ( ( Calautti et al., 2024c ; Calautti et al., 2024b ) ). Consider a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , a tuple t ¯ ∈ 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \bar{t}\in\mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} , and a database D ′ ⊆ D D^{\prime}\subseteq D . The following are equivalent: (1) There is a proof tree (resp., an unambiguous proof tree) T T of R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) R(\bar{t}) w.r.t. D D and Σ \Sigma with support D ′ D^{\prime} . (2) There is a proof DAG (resp., an unambiguous proof DAG) G = ( V , E , λ ) G=(V,E,\lambda) of R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) R(\bar{t}) w.r.t. D D and Σ \Sigma with support D ′ D^{\prime} such that the following hold: (a) For each v ∈ V v\in V , λ ⁡ ( v ) \lambda(v) is a node of 𝖽𝗈𝗐𝗇 ⁡ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , D , Σ ) \mathsf{down}(R(\bar{t}),D,\Sigma) . (b) For each v ∈ V v\in V with outgoing edges ( v , u 1 ) , … , ( v , u n ) (v,u_{1}),\ldots,(v,u_{n}) , ( λ ⁡ ( v ) , { λ ⁡ ( u 1 ) , … , λ ⁡ ( u n ) } ) (\lambda(v),\{\lambda(u_{1}),\ldots,\lambda(u_{n})\}) belongs to 𝖽𝗈𝗐𝗇 ⁡ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , D , Σ ) \mathsf{down}(R(\bar{t}),D,\Sigma) . (c) For each fact α \alpha , it holds that | { v ∈ V ∣ λ ⁡ ( v ) = α } | ≤ 𝖻𝗈𝗎𝗇𝖽 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , D , Σ ) |\{v\in V\mid\lambda(v)=\alpha\}|\leq\mathsf{bound}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(R(\bar{t}),D,\Sigma) (resp., 𝖻𝗈𝗎𝗇𝖽 𝖴𝖭 ​ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , D , Σ ) \mathsf{bound}_{\mathsf{UN}}(R(\bar{t}),D,\Sigma) ). Let us now discuss how Theorem 6.9 can be used in order to devise an ILP encoding of why-provenance. Graph-based ILP Encoding Fix a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , a tuple t ¯ ∈ 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \bar{t}\in\mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} , and let 𝖽𝗈𝗐𝗇 ⁡ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , D , Σ ) = ( V , E ) \mathsf{down}(R(\bar{t}),D,\Sigma)=(V,E) . We start with the ILP encoding for 𝗐𝗁𝗒 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) , which we dub the graph-based ILP encoding of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) , and denote it by 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{graph\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) . The encoding is a direct implementation of Theorem 6.9 , namely the set of constraints 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{graph\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) searches for a proof DAG of R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) R(\bar{t}) w.r.t. D D and Σ \Sigma with some support, where no more than 𝖻𝗈𝗎𝗇𝖽 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , D , Σ ) \mathsf{bound}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(R(\bar{t}),D,\Sigma) nodes are labeled with the same fact. Formally, we construct 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{graph\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) as a system of constraints over integer variables X X and binary variables B B as follows. The Variables of 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{graph\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) . Let E ^ \hat{E} be the set of (standard) edges induced by the hyperedges of 𝖽𝗈𝗐𝗇 ⁡ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , D , Σ ) \mathsf{down}(R(\bar{t}),D,\Sigma) , i.e., E ^ = { ( α , β ) ∣ ( α , { … , β , … } ) ∈ E } \hat{E}=\{(\alpha,\beta)\mid(\alpha,\{\ldots,\beta,\ldots\})\in E\} . For a fact α \alpha , an amplified copy of α \alpha is an expression of the form α i \alpha^{i} , where i ∈ [ 𝖻𝗈𝗎𝗇𝖽 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , D , Σ ) ] i\in[\mathsf{bound}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(R(\bar{t}),D,\Sigma)] if α ∉ D \alpha\not\in D , and i = 1 i=1 if α ∈ D \alpha\in D . In other words, a database fact admits a single amplified copy. Moreover, for a hyperedge ( α , T ) ∈ E (\alpha,T)\in E , with T = { β 1 , … , β n } T=\{\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{n}\} , of 𝖽𝗈𝗐𝗇 ⁡ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , D , Σ ) \mathsf{down}(R(\bar{t}),D,\Sigma) , an amplified copy of ( α , T ) (\alpha,T) is an expression of the form ( α i , T ′ ) (\alpha^{i},T^{\prime}) , with T ′ = { β 1 k 1 , … , β n k n } T^{\prime}=\{\beta_{1}^{k_{1}},\ldots,\beta_{n}^{k_{n}}\} , where α i \alpha^{i} is an amplified copy of α \alpha , and β j k j \beta_{j}^{k_{j}} is an amplified copy of β j \beta_{j} , for j ∈ [ n ] j\in[n] . We now introduce the variables of 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{graph\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) . The set X X is empty, whereas B B is the union of three disjoint sets B N B_{N} , B H B_{H} , and B E B_{E} defined as follows: - The set B N B_{N} contains a binary variable x α i x_{\alpha^{i}} for each amplified copy α i \alpha^{i} of a fact α ∈ V ∪ D \alpha\in V\cup D . - The set B H B_{H} contains a binary variable y ( α i , T ′ ) y_{(\alpha^{i},T^{\prime})} for each amplified copy ( α i , T ′ ) (\alpha^{i},T^{\prime}) of a hyperedge ( α , T ) ∈ E (\alpha,T)\in E . - The set B E B_{E} contains a binary variable z ( α i , β j ) z_{(\alpha^{i},\beta^{j})} for each pair of amplified copies α i , β j \alpha^{i},\beta^{j} of facts α , β \alpha,\beta such that ( α , β ) ∈ E ^ (\alpha,\beta)\in\hat{E} . Intuitively, when x α i x_{\alpha^{i}} is true, for a fact α ∈ V ∪ D \alpha\in V\cup D , it means that a node of the underlying proof DAG G G is labeled with α \alpha , and among all nodes of G G labeled with α \alpha , this node has i i as its identifier. In other words, α i \alpha^{i} is the unique name of such a node labeled with α \alpha in G G . Moreover, the variables of B N B_{N} and B E B_{E} that become true via a solution of 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , D , Σ ) \mathsf{graph\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(R(\bar{t}),D,\Sigma) induce the nodes and the edges of a proof DAG G G for R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) R(\bar{t}) w.r.t. D D and Σ \Sigma , where each true variable of the form x α i x_{\alpha^{i}} means that among all possible nodes of a proof DAG that can be labeled with α \alpha , the node with identifier i i is part of G G , and a true variable of the form z ( α i , β j ) z_{(\alpha^{i},\beta^{j})} means that the node with identifier i i labeled with α \alpha and the node with identifier j j labeled with β \beta are connected by an edge in G G . The Constraints of 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{graph\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) . We now move to the constraints. In particular, the system 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{graph\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}}(\bar{t},D,Q) is a set of constraints of the form T 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 ∪ T 𝗋𝗈𝗈𝗍 ∪ T 𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗈𝖿 ∪ T 𝖺𝖼𝗒𝖼𝗅𝗂𝖼 . T_{\mathsf{graph}}\cup T_{\mathsf{root}}\cup T_{\mathsf{proof}}\cup T_{\mathsf{acyclic}}. The set of constraints T 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 T_{\mathsf{graph}} is in charge of guaranteeing consistency between the truth value of the variables in B N B_{N} and the variables in B E B_{E} , i.e., if an edge between two nodes is part of G G , then the two nodes must belong to G G as well. Formally, T 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 T_{\mathsf{graph}} is the set { z ( α i , β j ) ≤ x α i ∣ z ( α i , β j ) ∈ B E } ∪ { z ( α i , β j ) ≤ x β j ∣ z ( α i , β j ) ∈ B E } . \left\{z_{(\alpha^{i},\beta^{j})}\leq x_{\alpha^{i}}\mid z_{(\alpha^{i},\beta^{j})}\in B_{E}\right\}\ \cup\ \left\{z_{(\alpha^{i},\beta^{j})}\leq x_{\beta^{j}}\mid z_{(\alpha^{i},\beta^{j})}\in B_{E}\right\}. The set of constraints T 𝗋𝗈𝗈𝗍 T_{\mathsf{root}} guarantees that G G contains a distinguished node labeled with the fact R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) R(\bar{t}) , which is the root of G G , and no other node of G G can be the root (i.e., every other node must have at least one incoming edge). For this, we pick R ​ ( t ¯ ) 1 R(\bar{t})^{1} , which we denote as ρ \rho , as the representative node labeled with R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) R(\bar{t}) to play the role of the root. Formally, T 𝗋𝗈𝗈𝗍 T_{\mathsf{root}} is the set { x ρ = 1 } ∪ { z ( α i , ρ ) = 0 ∣ z ( α i , ρ ) ∈ B E } ∪ { x α i ≤ ∑ z ( β j , α i ) ∈ B E z ( β j , α i ) ∣ x α i ∈ B N ​ with ​ α ∈ V ​ and ​ α i ≠ ρ } . \{x_{\rho}=1\}\cup\left\{z_{(\alpha^{i},\rho)}=0\mid z_{(\alpha^{i},\rho)}\in B_{E}\right\}\cup\\ \left\{x_{\alpha^{i}}\leq\sum\limits_{z_{(\beta^{j},\alpha^{i})}\in B_{E}}z_{(\beta^{j},\alpha^{i})}\mid x_{\alpha^{i}}\in B_{N}\text{ with }\alpha\in V\text{ and }\alpha^{i}\neq\rho\right\}. We now discuss T 𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗈𝖿 T_{\mathsf{proof}} . Roughly, this set of constraints is in charge of guaranteeing that the nodes and edges induced by the true variables of B N B_{N} and B E B_{E} form a valid proof DAG. For this, the constraints ensure, for each fact α ∈ D ∖ V \alpha\in D\setminus V , that each variable of the form x α i x_{\alpha^{i}} is always false, and, for all other facts α ∈ V \alpha\in V , ensure that (i) when a node α i \alpha^{i} belongs to G G , i.e., it is a node labeled with α \alpha , and (ii) α \alpha is an intensional atom α \alpha , then α i \alpha^{i} must have the correct children in G G . The latter means that the labels of the children of α i \alpha^{i} form the target of some hyperedge of 𝖽𝗈𝗐𝗇 ⁡ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , D , Q ) \mathsf{down}(R(\bar{t}),D,Q) having α \alpha as the source. Moreover, no other nodes can be the children of α i \alpha^{i} . This is achieved with two families of constraints in T 𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗈𝖿 T_{\mathsf{proof}} . The first set of constraints is in charge of choosing which nodes should the children of α i \alpha^{i} in G G , assuming α i \alpha^{i} occurs in G G . This is done by forcing one of the variables of the form y ( α i , T ) ∈ B H y_{(\alpha^{i},T)}\in B_{H} to be true, whenever x α i x_{\alpha^{i}} is true. The second set of constraints guarantees that whenever the variable y ( α i , T ) ∈ B H y_{(\alpha^{i},T)}\in B_{H} is true, all and only the nodes in T T are children of α i \alpha^{i} in G G . Formally, T 𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗈𝖿 T_{\mathsf{proof}} is the set constraints { x α i = 0 ∣ α ∈ D ∖ V } ∪ { x α i ≤ ∑ y ( α i , T ) ∈ B H y ( α i , T ) ∣ x α i ∈ B N ​ with ​ α ∈ V ​ intensional } ∪ { y e ≤ ℓ e , β j ∣ y e ∈ B H ​ with ​ e = ( α i , T ) ​ and ​ z ( α i , β j ) ∈ B E } , \left\{x_{\alpha^{i}}=0\mid\alpha\in D\setminus V\right\}\cup\\ \left\{x_{\alpha^{i}}\leq\sum\limits_{y_{(\alpha^{i},T)}\in B_{H}}y_{(\alpha^{i},T)}\mid x_{\alpha^{i}}\in B_{N}\text{ with }\alpha\in V\text{ intensional }\right\}\cup\\ \left\{y_{e}\leq\ell_{e,\beta^{j}}\mid y_{e}\in B_{H}\text{ with }e=(\alpha^{i},T)\text{ and }z_{(\alpha^{i},\beta^{j})}\in B_{E}\right\}, where, for each e = ( α i , T ) e=(\alpha^{i},T) , ℓ e , β j \ell_{e,\beta^{j}} denotes z ( α i , β j ) z_{(\alpha^{i},\beta^{j})} if β j ∈ T \beta^{j}\in T , and 1 − z ( α i , β j ) 1-z_{(\alpha^{i},\beta^{j})} otherwise. We finally discuss T 𝖺𝖼𝗒𝖼𝗅𝗂𝖼 T_{\mathsf{acyclic}} , which is in charge of checking that G G , namely the graph whose edges correspond to the true variables in B E B_{E} , is acyclic. Checking the acyclicity of a graph via a set of constraints over binary variables defining the edges of the graph is a well-studied problem in different fields with a plethora of encodings. For our construction, we employ the state-of-the-art encoding based on vertex elimination ( Rankooh and Rintanen, 2022 ) , which is much more efficient than other encodings that compute the full transitive closure of the graph. sections.heading: 7. Exact Computation of Diverse Why-Provenance
sections.text: In the previous section, for each ⋆ ∈ { 𝖠𝖫𝖫 , 𝖴𝖭 } \star\in\{\mathsf{ALL},\mathsf{UN}\} , we introduced two different strategies for constructing ILP encodings for 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) , given a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , and a tuple t ¯ ∈ 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \bar{t}\in\mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} . This in turn led to four concrete instantiations of the generic algorithm 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ 𝖡𝗎𝗂𝗅𝖽𝖨𝖫𝖯𝖤𝗇𝖼 ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{BuildILPEnc}] of Algorithm 1 discussed in Section 5 , by choosing 𝖡𝗎𝗂𝗅𝖽𝖨𝖫𝖯𝖤𝗇𝖼 ∈ { 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 , 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 , 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖴𝖭 , 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖴𝖭 } \mathsf{BuildILPEnc}\in\{\mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}},\mathsf{graph\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}},\mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{UN}},\mathsf{graph\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{UN}}\} . This provides two algorithms for solving 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ - ​ 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \mathsf{ALL}\text{-}\mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} , and two algorithms for solving 𝖴𝖭 ​ - ​ 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \mathsf{UN}\text{-}\mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} . The goal of this section is to experimentally evaluate those algorithms. In the rest of the section, we will first discuss how we implemented the algorithms in question, and then present an experimental evaluation of such implementations. The latter will allow us to assess the running time of our implementations on well-established benchmarks, and, in particular, how the running time scales w.r.t. the requested number k k of members of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) .

sections.heading: 7.1. Implementation Details
sections.text: In what follows, fix a family of proof trees ⋆ ∈ { 𝖠𝖫𝖫 , 𝖴𝖭 } \star\in\{\mathsf{ALL},\mathsf{UN}\} , and a desired charaterization γ ∈ { 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 , 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 } \gamma\in\{\mathsf{hyper},\mathsf{graph}\} . We recall that for a given Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , database D D , and tuple t ¯ \bar{t} , constructing the ILP encoding γ ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{\gamma\text{-}ILP}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) requires first the construction of the downward closure 𝖽𝗈𝗐𝗇 ⁡ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , D , Σ ) \mathsf{down}(R(\bar{t}),D,\Sigma) . Hence, the main tasks that the algorithm 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ γ ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 ⋆ ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{\gamma\text{-}ILP}_{\star}] needs to perform can be summarized as follows: (1) compute 𝖽𝗈𝗐𝗇 ⁡ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , D , Σ ) \mathsf{down}(R(\bar{t}),D,\Sigma) , (2) compute the encoding T = γ ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) T=\mathsf{\gamma\text{-}ILP}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) , together with the ( T , k ) (T,k) -problem ( f , S ) (f,S) , by using 𝖽𝗈𝗐𝗇 ⁡ ( R ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , D , Σ ) \mathsf{down}(R(\bar{t}),D,\Sigma) , and (3) solve ( f , S ) (f,S) . We briefly describe how we implemented the above steps. Constructing the Downward Closure. Regarding the downward closure, this is a data structure that is orthogonal to the specific ILP encoding employed, and it has already been used in previous works on why-provenance for Datalog ( Elhalawati et al., 2022 ; Calautti et al., 2024b ) . In particular, we employ an existing implementation from ( Calautti et al., 2024b ) for computing the downward closure which in turn exploits the DLV Datalog engine ( Adrian et al., 2018 ) . Constructing the ILP Encoding. The construction of the ILP encoding T = γ ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) T=\mathsf{\gamma\text{-}ILP}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) and the corresponding ( T , k ) (T,k) -problem mostly follows their definition. The only differences are related to the database variables of T T and how we encode indicator constraints. Regarding the database variables, only the ones corresponding to facts appearing in the downward closure are actually generated in T T since, by definition of T = γ ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) T=\mathsf{\gamma\text{-}ILP}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) , all other database variables are always set to 0 0 , in any solution of T T , and thus the corresponding database facts will never appear in the output of 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ γ ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 ⋆ ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{\gamma\text{-}ILP}_{\star}] . Regarding the indicator constraints, these only occur in T T when γ = 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 \gamma=\mathsf{hyper} , and they are all of the form z ≡ ( a 1 x 1 + ⋯ a n x n ) ≥ 1 , z\ \equiv\ (\ a_{1}x_{1}+\cdots a_{n}x_{n}\ )\geq 1, where the expression a 1 x 1 + ⋯ a n x n a_{1}x_{1}+\cdots a_{n}x_{n} can never be negative and it is always an integer. Hence, the indicator constraint essentially asks that z z is 1 1 when a 1 x 1 + ⋯ a n x n a_{1}x_{1}+\cdots a_{n}x_{n} is non-zero, and zero when a 1 x 1 + ⋯ a n x n a_{1}x_{1}+\cdots a_{n}x_{n} is zero. For efficiency reasons, we encode the constraint by means of the following set of two constraints: { z ⋅ ( a 1 x 1 + ⋯ a n x n ) = a 1 x 1 + ⋯ a n x n , z ≤ a 1 x 1 + ⋯ a n x n } . \{z\cdot(\ a_{1}x_{1}+\cdots a_{n}x_{n}\ )=a_{1}x_{1}+\cdots a_{n}x_{n},\,\,\,z\leq a_{1}x_{1}+\cdots a_{n}x_{n}\}. We note that the first constraint is non-linear, due to the product on the left of the equality, and it might seem that this would result in a harder encoding w.r.t. a standard encoding via linear constraints. However, we recall that the standard encoding for the indicator constraint via linear constraints requires finding a constant M M that is guaranteed to be larger than a 1 x 1 + ⋯ a n x n a_{1}x_{1}+\cdots a_{n}x_{n} , for all values of x 1 , … , x n x_{1},\ldots,x_{n} . A preliminary analysis has shown that such a constant M M would be extremely large, and caused numerical instabilities while solving the ILP encodings, and thus cannot be employed for our implementation. Nonetheless, as we are going to see next, we will exploit a state-of-the-art solver that natively supports quadratic constraints, and thus, we can employ our alternative encoding. Finding Optimal Solutions. For solving the ( T , k ) (T,k) -problem ( f , S ) (f,S) built at the previous step, we use Gurobi ( Gurobi Optimization, LLC, 2026 ) , which is a state-of-the-art Mixed-Integer (Quadratic) Programming solver. sections.heading: 7.2. Experimental Setup
sections.text: System Details. All experiments were conducted on a server running Fedora Linux 39 (Cloud Edition), provisioned with 20 vCPUs (Intel Xeon Processor, Cascadelake) and 117GB of RAM. The algorithms 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ γ ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 ⋆ ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{\gamma\text{-}ILP}_{\star}] , with ⋆ ∈ { 𝖠𝖫𝖫 , 𝖴𝖭 } \star\in\{\mathsf{ALL},\mathsf{UN}\} and γ ∈ { 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 , 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 } \gamma\in\{\mathsf{hyper},\mathsf{graph}\} , are implemented in C++, apart from the step solving the maximization problem ( f , S ) (f,S) that is delegated to Gurobi 11.0.0 ( Gurobi Optimization, LLC, 2026 ) . We only use Java OpenJDK 21.0.11 as a thin wrapper around the C++ implementation to ease the logging of the results. Experimental Scenarios. We consider a variety of scenarios from the Datalog literature, where each scenario consists of a query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) and a family of databases 𝒟 \mathcal{D} over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) . All the considered scenarios are listed in Table 1 ; the number of rules in Σ \Sigma , whether the program Σ \Sigma is recursive or not, and further references about each scenario are given in the table as well. Let us provide further details about the adopted scenarios: 𝖳𝗋𝖺𝗇𝗌𝖢𝗅𝗈𝗌𝗎𝗋𝖾 \mathsf{TransClosure} .: This scenario computes the transitive closure of a graph and asks for connected nodes. The database 𝖻𝗂𝗍𝖼𝗈𝗂𝗇 \mathsf{bitcoin} stores a portion of the Bicoin network ( Weber et al., 2019 ) , and 𝖿𝖺𝖼𝖾𝖻𝗈𝗈𝗄 \mathsf{facebook} stores different “social circles” from Facebook ( McAuley and Leskovec, 2012 ) . 𝖣𝗈𝖼𝗍𝗈𝗋𝗌 \mathsf{Doctors} .: The scenarios 𝖽𝗈𝖼𝗍𝗈𝗋𝗌 ​ - ​ i \mathsf{doctors\text{-}}i , for i ∈ [ 7 ] i\in[7] , represent queries obtained from a well-known data-exchange benchmark involving existential rules (the existential variables have been replaced with fresh constants). All such scenarios share the same database with 100K facts. 𝖦𝖺𝗅𝖾𝗇 \mathsf{Galen} .: This scenario implements the ELK calculus ( Kazakov et al., 2014 ) and asks for all pairs of concepts that are related with the 𝗌𝗎𝖻𝖢𝗅𝖺𝗌𝗌𝖮𝖿 \mathsf{subClassOf} relation. The various databases contain different portions of the Galen ontology ( The Oxford Library, 2007 ) . 𝖢𝖲𝖣𝖠 \mathsf{CSDA} .: This scenario (Context-Sensitive Dataflow Analysis) implements the Andersen “points-to” algorithm for determining the flow of data in procedural programs and asks for null references in a program. The databases 𝗁𝗍𝗍𝗉𝖽 \mathsf{httpd} , 𝗉𝗈𝗌𝗍𝗀𝗋𝖾𝗌𝗊𝗅 {\mathsf{postgresql}} , and 𝗅𝗂𝗇𝗎𝗑 {\mathsf{linux}} store the statements of the httpd web server, the PostgreSQL DBMS, and the Linux kernel, respectively. Execution. For each scenario s s , consisting of a query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) and a family of databases 𝒟 \mathcal{D} , we first computed Q ⁡ ( D ) Q(D) , for each database D ∈ 𝒟 D\in\mathcal{D} , using an off-the-shelf Datalog engine ( Adrian et al., 2018 ) , and selected 100 100 tuples t ¯ s , D 1 , … , t ¯ s , D 100 \bar{t}^{1}_{s,D},\ldots,\bar{t}^{100}_{s,D} from Q ⁡ ( D ) Q(D) uniformly at random. Then, for the experimental evaluation, for each of the four combinations of proof tree family ⋆ ∈ { 𝖠𝖫𝖫 , 𝖴𝖭 } \star\in\{\mathsf{ALL},\mathsf{UN}\} and characterization γ ∈ { 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 , 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 } \gamma\in\{\mathsf{hyper},\mathsf{graph}\} , each scenario s s , each database D D of the scenario, each tuple t s , D i t^{i}_{s,D} , with i ∈ [ 100 ] i\in[100] , and each k ∈ [ 5 ] k\in[5] , we executed our implementation of the algorithm 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ γ ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 ⋆ ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{\gamma\text{-}ILP}_{\star}] with input Q Q , D D , t ¯ s , D i \bar{t}^{i}_{s,D} , and k k . We collected the total running time, and the diversity of the resulting set, providing that the execution did not fail. Each execution had a timeout of 10 minutes.

sections.heading: 7.3. Experimental Results
sections.text: Before we discuss the results of our experimental evaluation, we point out that for the ILP encoding 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 \mathsf{graph\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}} , all executions of the algorithm 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{graph\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}}] did not terminate withing the given timeout. This is due to the extremely high number of variables that are required by the ILP encoding 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 \mathsf{graph\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}} . The latter is due to the very high number of amplified copies of facts and hyperedges. For this reason, although we will discuss the results related to all our algorithms, we will only present plots for the remaining 3 algorithms 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}}] , 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖴𝖭 ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{UN}}] , and 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖴𝖭 ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{graph\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{UN}}] . Visualizing Our Results. For each scenario s = ( Q , 𝒟 ) s=(Q,\mathcal{D}) , database D ∈ 𝒟 D\in\mathcal{D} , k ∈ [ 5 ] k\in[5] , and algorithm 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ γ ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 ⋆ ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{\gamma\text{-}ILP}_{\star}] , with ( γ , ⋆ ) ∈ { ( 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 , 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ) (\gamma,\star)\in\{(\mathsf{hyper},\mathsf{ALL}) , ( 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 , 𝖴𝖭 ) (\mathsf{hyper},\mathsf{UN}) , ( 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 , 𝖴𝖭 ) } (\mathsf{graph},\mathsf{UN})\} , we report the runtimes of the executions of the algorithm 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ γ ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 ⋆ ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{\gamma\text{-}ILP}_{\star}] with input the query Q Q , the database D D , one of the tuples t ¯ s , D i \bar{t}^{i}_{s,D} for i ∈ [ 100 ] i\in[100] , and the parameter k k , in a dedicated box-plot. In particular, each box-plot reports only the runtimes for the tuples t ¯ s , D i \bar{t}^{i}_{s,D} that have at least 5 members in 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ s , D i , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t}^{i}_{s,D},D,Q) . The reason for this is that answer tuples with, e.g., no more than 2 2 explanations would be reported with an identical running time, for all 2 < k ≤ 5 2<k\leq 5 , thus biasing the comparison across different values of k k . Nonetheless, out of the 100 randomly selected answer tuples, this filtering retained 6 tuples for bitcoin , 68 for facebook , 77 for httpd , 57 for linux , 55 for postgresql , and all 100 tuples for each of the seven doctors scenarios. We treat galen differently because most tuples t ¯ s , D i \bar{t}^{i}_{s,D} had only one member in 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ s , D i , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t}^{i}_{s,D},D,Q) . Thus, for galen , we report execution times only for k = 1 k=1 , retaining all 100 sampled tuples for each of the databases D 15 D_{15} , D 25 D_{25} , D 40 D_{40} , and D 50 D_{50} . The box-plots are organized in figures and subfigures as follows. Each figure, from Figure 1 to Figure 5 , collects the box-plots relative to a specific scenario s = ( Q , 𝒟 ) s=(Q,\mathcal{D}) . Each figure has a subfigure for each database D ∈ 𝒟 D\in\mathcal{D} of the scenario s s , which shows the box-plots relative to the execution of each of the algorithms 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ γ ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 ⋆ ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{\gamma\text{-}ILP}_{\star}] , with ( γ , ⋆ ) ∈ { ( 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 , 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ) (\gamma,\star)\in\{(\mathsf{hyper},\mathsf{ALL}) , ( 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 , 𝖴𝖭 ) (\mathsf{hyper},\mathsf{UN}) , ( 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 , 𝖴𝖭 ) } (\mathsf{graph},\mathsf{UN})\} , over the tuples t ¯ s , D i \bar{t}^{i}_{s,D} having at least 5 members of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ s , D i , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t}^{i}_{s,D},D,Q) , for the different values of k ∈ [ 5 ] k\in[5] . Since for galen we focus only on the case of k = 1 k=1 , we group in each subfigure relative to a database D ∈ 𝒟 D\in\mathcal{D} , all the box-plots relative to the three algorithms, executed with k = 1 k=1 . In each box-plot, the bottom and the top borders represent the first and third quartile, i.e., the runtime under which 25% and 75% of all the runtimes occur, respectively, and the middle line represents the median runtime. Moreover, the bottom and the top whiskers represent the minimum and maximum runtime, respectively. Each box-plot also shows each individual runtime as a dot, where red dots denote timeouts, and the percentage of tuples for which a timeout was reached is shown in red on the box-plot as well. Finally, the overal distribution of the runtimes is shown around the box-plot by means of a violin plot; wider areas denote runtimes that are more frequent across the considered tuples. Runtimes are in milliseconds over a log-scale. Algorithms Comparison. We first provide a relative comparison of the algorithms 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ γ ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 ⋆ ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{\gamma\text{-}ILP}_{\star}] , for ⋆ ∈ { 𝖠𝖫𝖫 , 𝖴𝖭 } \star\in\{\mathsf{ALL},\mathsf{UN}\} , and γ ∈ { 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 , 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 } \gamma\in\{\mathsf{hyper},\mathsf{graph}\} . When focusing on ⋆ = 𝖠𝖫𝖫 \star=\mathsf{ALL} , and thus on the computation of diverse sets of k k members of the why-provenance relative to arbitrary proof trees, only the algorithm 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}}] is able to complete its execution in most of the scenarios, whereas 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{graph\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}}] timeouts in all scenarios, for all answer tuples, as already discussed at the beginning of the section. Hence, 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}}] is the way to go for solving 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ​ - ​ 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \mathsf{ALL}\text{-}\mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} . The picture is different for ⋆ = 𝖴𝖭 \star=\mathsf{UN} , i.e., when focusing on the family of unambiguous proof trees. In this case, both algorithms 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖴𝖭 ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{UN}}] and 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖴𝖭 ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{graph\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{UN}}] perform similarly across all scenarios, with the exception of the doctors scenarios, where the algorithm 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖴𝖭 ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{UN}}] is generally faster, while the algorithm 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖴𝖭 ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{graph\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{UN}}] exhibits higher runtimes and a higher number of timeouts. This difference is due to the fact that the ILP encoding 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖴𝖭 \mathsf{graph\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{UN}} employs the set of constraints T 𝖺𝖼𝗒𝖼𝗅𝗂𝖼 T_{\mathsf{acyclic}} whose size is highly sensitive on how connected the downward closure is. This is a consequence of the vertex elimination technique employed in T 𝖺𝖼𝗒𝖼𝗅𝗂𝖼 T_{\mathsf{acyclic}} . This is confirmed by Figure 6 , which reports the number of variables occurring in T 𝖺𝖼𝗒𝖼𝗅𝗂𝖼 T_{\mathsf{acyclic}} for each of the answer tuples considered in the three scenarios doctors 1, doctors 5, and doctors 7, which are the only doctors scenarios where 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖴𝖭 ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{graph\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{UN}}] starts exhibiting timeouts; the timeouts occur for k ∈ { 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 } k\in\{2,3,4,5\} , k ∈ { 4 , 5 } k\in\{4,5\} , and k ∈ { 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 } k\in\{2,3,4,5\} , respectively. In the plots, red dots denote answer tuples for which a timeout is reached. The box-plots clearly show that timeouts consistently occur for tuples in which the number of variables employed in T 𝖺𝖼𝗒𝖼𝗅𝗂𝖼 T_{\mathsf{acyclic}} is higher. From the above discussion, we conclude that in the case of unambiguous proof trees, the algorithms 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖴𝖭 ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{hyper\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{UN}}] and 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖴𝖭 ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{graph\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{UN}}] are generally comparable, but the first is to be preferred for a more predictable running time. Runtimes for the csda scenario. Figure 6 . Number of variables occurring in the set T 𝖺𝖼𝗒𝖼𝗅𝗂𝖼 T_{\mathsf{acyclic}} of the ILP encoding 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖴𝖭 \mathsf{graph\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{UN}} . Red dots denote timeouts. Runtime Evaluation and Scalability with the Diversity Parameter. We now analyse the running time of our algorithms in absolute terms, and their scalability w.r.t. the input diversity parameter k k . Our results show that, apart from 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{graph\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}}] , which timeouts in all scenarios, 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ γ ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 ⋆ ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{\gamma\text{-}ILP}_{\star}] , with ( γ , ⋆ ) ∈ { ( 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 , 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ) (\gamma,\star)\in\{(\mathsf{hyper},\mathsf{ALL}) , ( 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 , 𝖴𝖭 ) (\mathsf{hyper},\mathsf{UN}) , ( 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 , 𝖴𝖭 ) } (\mathsf{graph},\mathsf{UN})\} , perform well across all scenarios when computing sets of no more than k = 3 k=3 maximally diverse explanations. In this setting, such sets can be computed in the order of seconds in most cases, with some scenarios requiring some minutes, for most of the answer tuples. For larger values of k k , runtimes stay below the 10-minutes timeout for the less demanding scenarios (Figure 1 / bitcoin , Figure 2 , and Figure 4 ), while an increasibly large number of timeouts can be observed for the more demanding scenarios (Figure 1 / facebook , and Figure 5 ), even when focusing on the best performing algorithm for each family of proof trees. Hence, all the algorithms we consider do not scale well with k k , in general. This is due to the exponential growth of the search space of the underlying maximization problem solved by each of the algorithms we consider. Indeed, there are ( N k ) \binom{N}{k} possible sets of k k explanations to consider, where N N is the total number of explanations in 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) , which itself can already be exponentially large w.r.t. | D | |D| , for a considered query Q Q , database D D , and tuple t ¯ \bar{t} . From our discussion, we conclude that although the above three algorithms are effective at finding diverse sets of small size, they exhibit poor scalability w.r.t. the diversity parameter k k , and thus, they quickly become infeasible for computing larger sets. This motivates the need for alternative approaches that trade optimality of the computed sets for performance, namely for approximation techniques. This will be the subjected of the next section.

sections.heading: 8. Approximation Algorithm for Diverse Why-Provenance
sections.text: We proceed to present an approximation algorithm for the problem ⋆ - ​ 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \star\text{-}\mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} , where ⋆ ∈ { 𝖠𝖫𝖫 , 𝖴𝖭 } \star\in\{\mathsf{ALL},\mathsf{UN}\} . Our goal is to devise an algorithm that, given as input a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , a tuple t ¯ ∈ 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \bar{t}\in\mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} , and k > 0 k>0 , computes a set of 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ k ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}^{k}(\bar{t},D,Q) whose diversity is an approximation of the optimal diversity and it performs much faster, in practice, than the approach discussed in Section 6 that aims for an exact computation. We first formalize the kind of approximation algorithm that we target and then explain how we obtain such an algorithm. Definition 8.1. For any β ≥ 1 \beta\geq 1 , a β \beta -approximation algorithm for ⋆ - ​ 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \star\text{-}\mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} , where ⋆ ∈ { 𝖠𝖫𝖫 , 𝖴𝖭 } \star\in\{\mathsf{ALL},\mathsf{UN}\} , is an algorithm that, given as input a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , a tuple t ¯ ∈ 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \bar{t}\in\mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} , and an integer k > 0 k>0 , outputs a set 𝒮 ^ ∈ 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ k ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \hat{\mathcal{S}}\in\mathsf{why}_{\star}^{k}(\bar{t},D,Q) of k k databases such that δ ⁡ ( 𝒮 ^ ) ≥ 1 β ⋅ δ ⁡ ( 𝒮 𝗈𝗉𝗍 ) , \delta(\hat{\mathcal{S}})\geq\dfrac{1}{\beta}\cdot\delta(\mathcal{S}_{\mathsf{opt}}), if there is 𝒮 𝗈𝗉𝗍 ∈ arg ​ max 𝒮 ∈ 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ k ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) ⁡ δ ​ ( 𝒮 ) \mathcal{S}_{\mathsf{opt}}\in\argmax\limits_{\mathcal{S}\in\mathsf{why}_{\star}^{k}(\bar{t},D,Q)}\delta(\mathcal{S}) ; otherwise, it fails. We call β \beta the approximation ratio of the algorithm. Diverse Why-Provenance as a Remote-Clique Problem. To devise the desired approximation algorithm, we first observe that ⋆ - ​ 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \star\text{-}\mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} can be seen as a (succinct) encoding of the remote-clique problem, a well-studied optimization problem in graph theory. Consider an edge-weighted, undirected graph G = ( V , E , w ) G=(V,E,w) , where w : E → ℕ w:E\rightarrow\mathbb{N} assigns a non-negative weight to each edge of G G . By abuse of notation, for an edge { u , v } ∈ E \{u,v\}\in E , we may write w ⁡ ( u , v ) w(u,v) or w ⁡ ( v , u ) w(v,u) instead of w ⁡ ( { u , v } ) w(\{u,v\}) . We further assume that w ⁡ ( v , v ) = 0 w(v,v)=0 , for each node v ∈ V v\in V . We say that G G is complete if, for every pair of distinct nodes u , v ∈ V u,v\in V , there is an edge { u , v } ∈ E \{u,v\}\in E . For an edge-weighted, complete, undirected graph G = ( V , E , w ) G=(V,E,w) , we say that w w satisfies the triangle inequality if, for every three nodes v 1 , v 2 , v 3 ∈ V v_{1},v_{2},v_{3}\in V , w ⁡ ( v 1 , v 3 ) ≤ w ⁡ ( v 1 , v 2 ) + w ⁡ ( v 2 , v 3 ) w(v_{1},v_{3})\leq w(v_{1},v_{2})+w(v_{2},v_{3}) . For an integer k > 0 k>0 , we denote by 𝖼𝗅𝗂𝗊𝗎𝖾𝗌 k ​ ( G ) \mathsf{cliques}^{k}(G) the family of all sets V ′ ⊆ V V^{\prime}\subseteq V of k k nodes of G G . Finally, for a set V ′ = { v 1 , … , v k } ∈ 𝖼𝗅𝗂𝗊𝗎𝖾𝗌 k ​ ( G ) V^{\prime}=\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{k}\}\in\mathsf{cliques}^{k}(G) , the diversity of V ′ V^{\prime} is defined as the integer δ ⁡ ( V ′ ) = ∑ i , j ∈ [ | V ′ | ] ​ and ​ i < j w ⁡ ( v i , v j ) . \delta(V^{\prime})=\sum\limits_{i,j\in[|V^{\prime}|]\text{ and }i<j}w(v_{i},v_{j}). The remote-clique problem is defined as follows: PROBLEM : 𝖱𝖾𝗆𝗈𝗍𝖾 ​ - ​ 𝖢𝗅𝗂𝗊𝗎𝖾 \mathsf{Remote\text{-}Clique} INPUT : A complete, edge-weighted, undirected graph G = ( V , E , w ) G=(V,E,w) , where w w satisfies the triangle inequality, and an integer k > 0 k>0 OUTPUT : A member of arg ​ max V ′ ∈ 𝖼𝗅𝗂𝗊𝗎𝖾𝗌 k ​ ( G ) ⁡ δ ​ ( V ′ ) \argmax\limits_{V^{\prime}\in\mathsf{cliques}^{k}(G)}\delta(V^{\prime}) if it exists; otherwise fail It is easy to see that the problem ⋆ - ​ 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \star\text{-}\mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} , where ⋆ ∈ { 𝖠𝖫𝖫 , 𝖴𝖭 } \star\in\{\mathsf{ALL},\mathsf{UN}\} , can be reduced to 𝖱𝖾𝗆𝗈𝗍𝖾 ​ - ​ 𝖢𝗅𝗂𝗊𝗎𝖾 \mathsf{Remote\text{-}Clique} . In particular, given a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , a database D ∈ 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) D\in\mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , a tuple t ¯ ∈ 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \bar{t}\in\mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} , and an integer k > 0 k>0 , we construct the edge-weighted, complete, undirected graph G = ( V , E , w ) G=(V,E,w) , where V = 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) V=\mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) and w ⁡ ( D 1 , D 2 ) = | Δ ⁡ ( D 1 , D 2 ) | w(D_{1},D_{2})=|\Delta(D_{1},D_{2})| , for each D 1 , D 2 ∈ V D_{1},D_{2}\in V . 3 3 3 The weight function w w defined as w ⁡ ( D 1 , D 2 ) = | Δ ⁡ ( D 1 , D 2 ) | w(D_{1},D_{2})=|\Delta(D_{1},D_{2})| satisfies the triangle inequality since, for any three sets A , B , C A,B,C , Δ ⁡ ( A , C ) ⊆ Δ ⁡ ( A , B ) ∪ Δ ⁡ ( B , C ) \Delta(A,C)\subseteq\Delta(A,B)\cup\Delta(B,C) . It is clear that the output of 𝖱𝖾𝗆𝗈𝗍𝖾 ​ - ​ 𝖢𝗅𝗂𝗊𝗎𝖾 \mathsf{Remote\text{-}Clique} with input the graph G G as defined above and the integer k k coincides with the output of ⋆ - ​ 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \star\text{-}\mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} with input Q Q , D D , t ¯ \bar{t} , and k k . Approximation Algorithm for 𝖱𝖾𝗆𝗈𝗍𝖾 ​ - ​ 𝖢𝗅𝗂𝗊𝗎𝖾 \mathsf{Remote\text{-}Clique} . Due to the connection between our problem and the 𝖱𝖾𝗆𝗈𝗍𝖾 ​ - ​ 𝖢𝗅𝗂𝗊𝗎𝖾 \mathsf{Remote\text{-}Clique} problem discussed above, we can exploit exiting approximation algorithms for 𝖱𝖾𝗆𝗈𝗍𝖾 ​ - ​ 𝖢𝗅𝗂𝗊𝗎𝖾 \mathsf{Remote\text{-}Clique} to provide an approximation algorithm for our problem. The state of the art approximation algorithm for 𝖱𝖾𝗆𝗈𝗍𝖾 ​ - ​ 𝖢𝗅𝗂𝗊𝗎𝖾 \mathsf{Remote\text{-}Clique} is a greedy algorithm defined as follows. Given an input G , k G,k of the problem 𝖱𝖾𝗆𝗈𝗍𝖾 ​ - ​ 𝖢𝗅𝗂𝗊𝗎𝖾 \mathsf{Remote\text{-}Clique} , the algorithm performs k k iterations, where at each iteration i ∈ [ k ] i\in[k] , the algorithm picks a node v i ∈ V v_{i}\in V such that v i v_{i} is different from all previously selected nodes v j v_{j} , with j < i j<i , and v i v_{i} is such that the quantity δ ⁡ ( { v 1 , … , v i } ) − δ ⁡ ( { v 1 , … , v i − 1 } ) \delta(\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{i}\})-\delta(\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{i-1}\}) is maximized, namely v i v_{i} maximizes the marginal diversity , i.e., the increase in diversity w.r.t. the set of nodes selected so far. For each i ∈ [ k ] i\in[k] , if a node v i v_{i} which is different from all nodes v j v_{j} , with j < i j<i cannot be found, the algorithm halts failing. If instead all k k iterations complete without failing, the algorithm outputs the set { v 1 , … , v k } \{v_{1},\ldots,v_{k}\} and halts. The above algorithm is a 2 2 -approximation algorithm for 𝖱𝖾𝗆𝗈𝗍𝖾 ​ - ​ 𝖢𝗅𝗂𝗊𝗎𝖾 \mathsf{Remote\text{-}Clique} , where for any β ≥ 1 \beta\geq 1 , a β \beta -approximation algorithm for 𝖱𝖾𝗆𝗈𝗍𝖾 ​ - ​ 𝖢𝗅𝗂𝗊𝗎𝖾 \mathsf{Remote\text{-}Clique} is an algorithm that, given G G and k k , outputs a set V ^ \hat{V} of k k nodes such that δ ⁡ ( V ^ ) ≥ 1 β ⋅ δ ⁡ ( V 𝗈𝗉𝗍 ) \delta(\hat{V})\geq\frac{1}{\beta}\cdot\delta(V_{\mathsf{opt}}) , if there is V 𝗈𝗉𝗍 ∈ arg ​ max V ′ ∈ 𝖼𝗅𝗂𝗊𝗎𝖾𝗌 k ​ ( G ) ⁡ δ ​ ( V ′ ) V_{\mathsf{opt}}\in\argmax\limits_{V^{\prime}\in\mathsf{cliques}^{k}(G)}\delta(V^{\prime}) ; otherwise, it fails. Moreover, the factor 2 2 is tight for the approximation algorithm, i.e., there exist families of inputs G , k G,k for which the algorithm returns a set V ^ \hat{V} of k k nodes with δ ⁡ ( V ^ ) = 1 2 ⋅ δ ⁡ ( V 𝗈𝗉𝗍 ) \delta(\hat{V})=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\delta(V_{\mathsf{opt}}) . Approximation Algorithm for Diverse Why-Provenance. A naive adaptation of the greedy 2 2 -approximation algorithm discussed above to the problem ⋆ - ​ 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \star\text{-}\mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} would be as follows: given a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , a tuple t ¯ ∈ 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \bar{t}\in\mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} , and an integer k > 0 k>0 , (1) first construct the set 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) , (2) then construct G = ( V , E , w ) G=(V,E,w) with V = 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) V=\mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) and w ⁡ ( D 1 , D 2 ) = | Δ ⁡ ( D 1 , D 2 ) | w(D_{1},D_{2})=|\Delta(D_{1},D_{2})| , for each D 1 , D 2 ∈ V D_{1},D_{2}\in V , and (3) execute the 2 2 -approximation algorithm for the problem 𝖱𝖾𝗆𝗈𝗍𝖾 ​ - ​ 𝖢𝗅𝗂𝗊𝗎𝖾 \mathsf{Remote\text{-}Clique} with input G , k G,k . It should not come as a surprise that this naive approach would never scale in practice since it requires the explicit construction of the whole graph G G , which in turn requires the construction of the whole set 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) upfront; the latter can be very large. Hence, we need a more sophisticated approach that does not require the explicit construction of the graph G G . Towards such a sophisticated approach, we need a clever strategy for selecting a node v i v_{i} at each iteration i ∈ [ k ] i\in[k] that maximizes the integer δ ⁡ ( { v 1 , … , v i } ) − δ ⁡ ( { v 1 , … , v i − 1 } ) \delta(\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{i}\})-\delta(\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{i-1}\}) . In terms of our problem, this means that we need a way, given an already constructed set of i − 1 i-1 databases D 1 , … , D i − 1 D_{1},\ldots,D_{i-1} from 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) , to construct a new database D i ∈ 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) D_{i}\in\mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) that differs from all D 1 , … , D i − 1 D_{1},\ldots,D_{i-1} , and the marginal diversity δ ⁡ ( { D 1 , … , D i } ) − δ ⁡ ( { D 1 , … , D i − 1 } ) \delta(\{D_{1},\ldots,D_{i}\})-\delta(\{D_{1},\ldots,D_{i-1}\}) is maximized. We discuss how this can be achieved without, of course, explicitly constructing the set 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) , by exploiting once again our ILP-based framework introduced above. Let ⋆ ∈ { 𝖠𝖫𝖫 , 𝖴𝖭 } \star\in\{\mathsf{ALL},\mathsf{UN}\} , and assume that 𝖡𝗎𝗂𝗅𝖽𝖨𝖫𝖯𝖤𝗇𝖼 \mathsf{BuildILPEnc} is a procedure that takes as input a triple ( t ¯ , D , Q ) (\bar{t},D,Q) , where Q Q is a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , D D is a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , and t ¯ \bar{t} a tuple of 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} , and constructs an ILP encoding for 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) . The approximation algorithm 𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑 ⁡ [ 𝖡𝗎𝗂𝗅𝖽𝖨𝖫𝖯𝖤𝗇𝖼 ] \mathsf{Approx}[\mathsf{BuildILPEnc}] , which is parameterized with the procedure 𝖡𝗎𝗂𝗅𝖽𝖨𝖫𝖯𝖤𝗇𝖼 \mathsf{BuildILPEnc} , is depicted in Algorithm 2 . Note that in the description of the algorithm, we write g μ , i g_{\mu,i} , for each i ∈ [ n ] i\in[n] , to denote the “opposite” of x α i x_{\alpha_{i}} w.r.t. μ \mu , i.e., the expression 1 − x α i 1-x_{\alpha_{i}} if μ ⁡ ( x α i ) = 1 \mu(x_{\alpha_{i}})=1 , and the expression x α i x_{\alpha_{i}} if μ ⁡ ( x α i ) = 0 \mu(x_{\alpha_{i}})=0 . We can show the following: Theorem 8.2. Let ⋆ ∈ { 𝖠𝖫𝖫 , 𝖴𝖭 } \star\in\{\mathsf{ALL},\mathsf{UN}\} , and assume that 𝖡𝗎𝗂𝗅𝖽𝖨𝖫𝖯𝖤𝗇𝖼 \mathsf{BuildILPEnc} is a procedure that takes as input a triple ( t ¯ , D , Q ) (\bar{t},D,Q) , where Q Q is a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , D D is a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , and t ¯ \bar{t} a tuple of 𝖽𝗈𝗆 ​ ( D ) 𝖺𝗋 ⁡ ( R ) \mathsf{dom}(D)^{\mathsf{ar}(R)} , and constructs an ILP encoding for 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) . Then, 𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑 ⁡ [ 𝖡𝗎𝗂𝗅𝖽𝖨𝖫𝖯𝖤𝗇𝖼 ] \mathsf{Approx}[\mathsf{BuildILPEnc}] is a 2 2 -approximation algorithm for the problem ⋆ - ​ 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \star\text{-}\mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} . sections.text: The aim of this section is to experimentally evaluate the approximation algorithms 𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑 ⁡ [ γ ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 ⋆ ] \mathsf{Approx}[\mathsf{\gamma\text{-}ILP}_{\star}] , where ⋆ ∈ { 𝖠𝖫𝖫 , 𝖴𝖭 } \star\in\{\mathsf{ALL},\mathsf{UN}\} and γ ∈ { 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 , 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 } \gamma\in\{\mathsf{hyper},\mathsf{graph}\} . Our goal is to assess both their efficiency and the quality of the sets of explanations that they produce. To this end, we employ the same scenarios as the ones used in Section 7 . In particular, in Section 9.1 , we evaluate the runtime of the algorithm 𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑 ⁡ [ γ ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 ⋆ ] \mathsf{Approx}[\mathsf{\gamma\text{-}ILP}_{\star}] over all answer tuples which guarantee at least five members of the why-provenance, as in Section 7 , and compare it with the ones of the exact algorithm 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ γ ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 ⋆ ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{\gamma\text{-}ILP}_{\star}] . In Section 9.2 , we evaluate the quality of the diversity of the sets of explanations constructed by 𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑 ⁡ [ γ ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 ⋆ ] \mathsf{Approx}[\mathsf{\gamma\text{-}ILP}_{\star}] by comparing it against the optimal value computed by 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ γ ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 ⋆ ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{\gamma\text{-}ILP}_{\star}] in Section 7 ; we only report the comparison for the answer tuples for which the exact algorithm could finish its execution within the given 10-minutes timeout. The comparison is performed by computing the ratio d 𝑜𝑝𝑡 d 𝑎𝑝𝑥 \frac{d_{\mathit{opt}}}{d_{\mathit{apx}}} between the optimal diversity d 𝑜𝑝𝑡 d_{\mathit{opt}} provided by the algorithm 𝖢𝗈𝗆𝗉𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾 ⁡ [ γ ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 ⋆ ] \mathsf{CompDiverse}[\mathsf{\gamma\text{-}ILP}_{\star}] and the approximate diversity d 𝑎𝑝𝑥 d_{\mathit{apx}} provided by the algorithm 𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑 ⁡ [ γ ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 ⋆ ] \mathsf{Approx}[\mathsf{\gamma\text{-}ILP}_{\star}] . Finally, in Section 9.3 , we study the scalability of the approximation algorithms for larger values of k k (beyond those considered in Section 7 ). sections.heading: 9.1. Runtime Analysis
sections.text: As already discussed in Section 7 , constructing the ILP encoding via 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 𝖠𝖫𝖫 \mathsf{graph\text{-}ILP}_{\mathsf{ALL}} requires more than the given 10-minutes timeout. Therefore, as in Section 7 , we only report plots for the remaining three approximation algorithms 𝖠𝗉𝗉𝗋𝗈𝗑 ⁡ [ γ ​ - ​ 𝖨𝖫𝖯 ⋆ ] \mathsf{Approx}[\mathsf{\gamma\text{-}ILP}_{\star}] with ( γ , ⋆ ) ∈ { ( 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 , 𝖠𝖫𝖫 ) , ( 𝗁𝗒𝗉𝖾𝗋 , 𝖴𝖭 ) , ( 𝗀𝗋𝖺𝗉𝗁 , 𝖴𝖭 ) } (\gamma,\star)\in\{(\mathsf{hyper},\mathsf{ALL}),(\mathsf{hyper},\mathsf{UN}),(\mathsf{graph},\mathsf{UN})\} . Figures 7 - 10 report the runtime of the above three approximation algorithms across all scenarios, following the same organization of Figures 1 - 5 . Note that for the galen scenario, most answer tuples have only k = 1 k=1 explanations. Thus, we do not report the runtime of the approximation algorithms for the galen scenario since, for k = 1 k=1 , the approximation algorithms solve the same maximization problem as their exact counterpart and the runtimes are identical. As we can observe, in contrast to the exact computation (Section 7 ), the approximate computation scales smoothly as k k increases and achieves substantial improvements in runtime. The key observation is that the runtime is reduced by several orders of magnitude across all settings. Even as k k increases, runtimes remain low, with the vast majority of runs completing well below 10 3 10^{3} milliseconds (i.e., under one second). This represents a dramatic improvement over the exact computation and demonstrates that the approximate computation is suitable for practical, interactive settings that require near-real-time responses. As expected, and similar to the exact algorithm, the runtime of the approximation algorithms increases with k k , reflecting its incremental nature: it constructs the set of explanations by building one explanation at the time and by maximizing the marginal diversity at each step. However, this growth remains modest and controlled since the algorithms can avoid the combinatorial explosion of the search space of the exact algorithms that, at each of the k k iterations, it coincides (in the worst case) with the set of candidate explanations from 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( t ¯ , D , Q ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}(\bar{t},D,Q) . A direct consequence of this improvement is that the vast majority of timeouts observed with exact algorithms disappear, and only a small number of more demanding instances still reach the timeout threshold. Regarding differences across the family of proof trees and the ILP encodings considered, we observe similar trends to those discussed for the exact algorithms in Section 7 , although the differences are significantly less pronounced due to the reduced search space.

sections.heading: 9.2. Quality of the Approximation
sections.text: We now assess the quality of the approximate solutions. Figures 11 - 12 report the ratio between the optimal diversity and the diversity achieved by the approximation algorithms. The closer the ratio is to one the better the approximate solution, where a ratio equal to one means that the approximation algorithm managed to construct an optimal set of explanations; the number on the middle line in each box-plot refers to the average ratio. As expected, the ratio is exactly one for k = 1 k=1 since any singleton explanation provides optimal diversity, i.e., diversity equal to zero. For larger values of k k , the ratio typically increases slightly above one, indicating a small divergence from the optimum. Moreover, all the three algorithms provide similar ratios across all scenarios, and thus, there is no clear preference w.r.t. the quality of approximation. A consistent pattern across all scenarios is that the ratio is highest for small values of k > 1 k>1 (often at k = 2 k=2 ), and then gradually decreases as k k increases. This behavior is due to the greedy nature of the approximation algorithm: early choices are made without knowledge of future choices, which may lead to suboptimal combinations when only a few explanations are selected. As k k grows, the solution space becomes more constrained, and the greedy choices align more closely with the optimum. Summing up, the ratios remain quite close to one in all cases, with an average ratio of almost one for k ≥ 3 k\geq 3 . The worst-case average ratio is 1.4 1.4 for k = 2 k=2 in the graphanalytics scenario with the facebook database. This ratio, however, is still 30% better than the theoretical approximation ratio established in Theorem 8.2 .

sections.heading: 9.3. Scalability to Larger Diversity Parameter
sections.text: To further assess scalability, we evaluate the approximation algorithms for values of k k up to 10 on all scenarios except for galen ; galen is excluded for the usual reason discussed above. In this evaluation, we keep the 10 minutes timeout and report the runtime required to complete the computation for the answer tuples that have at least 10 members of the why-provenance. The results in Figures 14 - 17 show that the approximation algorithms keep scaling gracefully even for larger k k . Although the runtime increases as expected with k k , the growth remains controlled and stable. This experiment demonstrates that all approximation algorithms provide a reliable and scalable solution to generate diverse why-provenance explanations. This, together with our analysis of the quality of the approximation, allows us to conclude that all three approximation algorithms provide practical solutions.

sections.heading: 10. Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we initiated the study of the problem of computing a small, sufficiently diverse subset of the set of why-provenance explanations of a certain answer of interest. After formalizing the problem in question as an optimization problem, and showing that it is intractable in data complexity, we focussed our efforts on the question whether ILP optimization solvers can be employed towards practical solutions. Our thorough analysis and experimental evaluation showed that the latter is achievable as long as we keep the requested set of explanations small, or we employ approximation algorithms (with error guarantees). An interesting direction for future research is to consider alternative diversity measures that are conceptually relevant and efficiently computable; the next natural choice is the min function. Another interesting diection for future work is to study the problem of interest for more expressive query langauges, in particular, Datalog queries with negation interprested according to the standard well-founded or stable model semantics from Logic Programming. Note that the basic problem of computing why-provenance explanations for such expressive query languages has been recently studied in ( Bogaerts et al., 2026 ) , and thus, we can build on the notions introduced in that paper.

sections.heading: A.1. Proof of Theorem 4.1
sections.text: We first introduce the decision problem of checking whether a fixed Datalog query has k k answers over a given database D D such that their diversity is above a certain threshold; we know from ( Merkl et al., 2025 ) that this is an NP-hard problem. We then reduce this problem via a polynomial-time Turing reduction to our problems, which in turn establishes Theorem 4.1 . Diverse Answers Consider an integer n > 0 n>0 . For an n n -tuple t ¯ = ( t 1 , … , t n ) \bar{t}=(t_{1},\ldots,t_{n}) , let t ¯ ​ [ i ] \bar{t}[i] be the term t i t_{i} , with i ∈ [ n ] i\in[n] . For two n n -tuples t ¯ \bar{t} and u ¯ \bar{u} , the Hamming distance between t ¯ \bar{t} and u ¯ \bar{u} , denoted 𝗁𝖽 ⁡ ( t ¯ , u ¯ ) \mathsf{hd}(\bar{t},\bar{u}) , is defined as the integer | { i ∈ [ n ] ∣ t ¯ ​ [ i ] ≠ u ¯ ​ [ i ] } | |\{i\in[n]\mid\bar{t}[i]\neq\bar{u}[i]\}| . Moreover, for a set 𝒜 = { t ¯ 1 , … , t ¯ k } \mathcal{A}=\{\bar{t}_{1},\ldots,\bar{t}_{k}\} of n n -tuples, the diversity of 𝒜 \mathcal{A} , denoted δ ⁡ ( 𝒜 ) \delta(\mathcal{A}) , is defined as ∑ i , j ∈ [ k ] ​ and ​ i < j 𝗁𝖽 ⁡ ( t ¯ i , t ¯ j ) . \sum\limits_{i,j\in[k]\text{ and }i<j}\mathsf{hd}(\bar{t}_{i},\bar{t}_{j}). For a Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , and an integer k > 0 k>0 , we define 𝖺𝗇𝗌 k ​ ( D , Q ) \mathsf{ans}^{k}(D,Q) as the collection of all sets 𝒜 ⊆ Q ⁡ ( D ) \mathcal{A}\subseteq Q(D) of tuples with | 𝒜 | = k |\mathcal{A}|=k . For a fixed Datalog query Q = ( Σ , R ) Q=(\Sigma,R) , we consider the following decision problem: PROBLEM : 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖠𝗇𝗌𝗐𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖢𝗁𝖾𝖼𝗄 ⁡ [ Q ] \mathsf{DiverseAnswersCheck}[Q] INPUT : A database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma) , an integer k > 0 k>0 encoded in unary, and an integer d ≥ 0 d\geq 0 QUESTION : Is there a set 𝒜 ∈ 𝖺𝗇𝗌 k ​ ( D , Q ) \mathcal{A}\in\mathsf{ans}^{k}(D,Q) with δ ⁡ ( 𝒜 ) ≥ d ​ ? \delta(\mathcal{A})\geq d? We know that there is a Datalog query for which the above problem is NP-hard; this is a consequence of ( Merkl et al., 2025 , Theorem 3.13) . Theorem A.1. 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖠𝗇𝗌𝗐𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖢𝗁𝖾𝖼𝗄 ⁡ [ Q ∗ ] \mathsf{DiverseAnswersCheck}[Q^{*}] is NP-complete, where Q ∗ = ( Σ ∗ , R ) Q^{*}=(\Sigma^{*},R) with Σ ∗ = { R ( x 1 , … , x 5 ) :– P ( x 1 , … , x 5 ) } \Sigma^{*}=\{R(x_{1},\ldots,x_{5})\ \text{:--}\ P(x_{1},\ldots,x_{5})\} . The Reduction Consider now the Datalog query Q ^ = ( Σ ^ , R ^ ) \hat{Q}=(\hat{\Sigma},\hat{R}) , where R ^ \hat{R} is a 0 0 -ary predicate and Σ ^ \hat{\Sigma} consists of the single rule R ^ :– P ( x 1 , … , x 5 ) , P 1 ( x 1 ) , … , P 5 ( x 5 ) . \hat{R}\ \text{:--}\ P(x_{1},\ldots,x_{5}),P_{1}(x_{1}),\ldots,P_{5}(x_{5}). We proceed to show that, for every ⋆ ∈ { 𝖠𝖫𝖫 , 𝖴𝖭 } \star\in\{\mathsf{ALL},\mathsf{UN}\} , there exists a polynomial-time Turing reduction from 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖠𝗇𝗌𝗐𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖢𝗁𝖾𝖼𝗄 ⁡ [ Q ∗ ] \mathsf{DiverseAnswersCheck}[Q^{*}] to ⋆ - ​ 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 ​ [ Q ^ ] \star\text{-}\mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance}[\hat{Q}] , i.e., there is a procedure with access to an oracle for the problem ⋆ - ​ 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 ​ [ Q ^ ] \star\text{-}\mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance}[\hat{Q}] that decides 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖠𝗇𝗌𝗐𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖢𝗁𝖾𝖼𝗄 ⁡ [ Q ∗ ] \mathsf{DiverseAnswersCheck}[Q^{*}] in polynomial time. Consider an input to 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖠𝗇𝗌𝗐𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖢𝗁𝖾𝖼𝗄 ⁡ [ Q ∗ ] \mathsf{DiverseAnswersCheck}[Q^{*}] , i.e., a database D D over 𝖾𝖽𝖻 ⁡ ( Σ ∗ ) \mathsf{edb}(\Sigma^{*}) , an integer k > 0 k>0 encoded in unary, and an integer d ≥ 0 d\geq 0 . The procedure deciding 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖠𝗇𝗌𝗐𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖢𝗁𝖾𝖼𝗄 ⁡ [ Q ∗ ] \mathsf{DiverseAnswersCheck}[Q^{*}] , which we dub 𝖣𝖾𝖼𝗂𝖽𝖾𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖠𝗇𝗌𝗐𝖾𝗋𝗌 \mathsf{DecideDiverseAnswers} , does the following: (1) Construct the database D ^ = D ∪ { P 1 ( t 1 ) , … , P 5 ( t 5 ) ∣ P ( t 1 , … , t 5 ) ∈ D } . \hat{D}\ =\ D\cup\{P_{1}(t_{1}),\ldots,P_{5}(t_{5})\mid P(t_{1},\ldots,t_{5})\in D\}. (2) Ask the oracle to compute some 𝒮 ^ ∈ arg ​ max 𝒮 ∈ 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ k ​ ( ( , , , , ) ⁡ δ ​ ( 𝒮 ) \mathcal{\hat{S}}\in\argmax\limits_{\mathcal{S}\in\mathsf{why}_{\star}^{k}((),\hat{D},\hat{Q})}\delta(\mathcal{S}) . (3) If the oracle returns fail , then reject. (4) Accept if δ ⁡ ( 𝒮 ^ ) ≥ k ⋅ ( k − 1 ) + 2 ⋅ d \delta(\mathcal{\hat{S}})\geq k\cdot(k-1)+2\cdot d ; otherwise, reject. Running Time. The procedure 𝖣𝖾𝖼𝗂𝖽𝖾𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖠𝗇𝗌𝗐𝖾𝗋𝗌 \mathsf{DecideDiverseAnswers} clearly runs in polynomial time since constructing D ^ \hat{D} only requires iterating over the facts in D D . Moreover, the set 𝒮 ^ \mathcal{\hat{S}} returned by the oracle, when it exists, contains linearly many elements w.r.t. the size of the encoding of k k , and each element in 𝒮 ^ \mathcal{\hat{S}} is no larger than | D ^ | |\hat{D}| . Finally, computing δ ⁡ ( 𝒮 ^ ) \delta(\mathcal{\hat{S}}) requires adding k ⁡ ( k − 1 ) k(k-1) symmetric distances, and the number k ⁡ ( k − 1 ) + 2 ⋅ d k(k-1)+2\cdot d can be easily computed. Correctness. We proceed to show that the procedure indeed decides 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖠𝗇𝗌𝗐𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖢𝗁𝖾𝖼𝗄 ⁡ [ Q ∗ ] \mathsf{DiverseAnswersCheck}[Q^{*}] . We first make some observations. For a 5 5 -tuple t ¯ \bar{t} , let D t ¯ = { P ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , P 1 ​ ( t ¯ ​ [ 1 ] ) , … , P 5 ​ ( t ¯ ​ [ 5 ] ) } D_{\bar{t}}=\{P(\bar{t}),P_{1}(\bar{t}[1]),\ldots,P_{5}(\bar{t}[5])\} . It is not difficult to verify that by construction of D ^ \hat{D} and by definition of Q ^ = ( Σ ^ , R ^ ) \hat{Q}=(\hat{\Sigma},\hat{R}) , we have that: Observation 1. For each ⋆ ∈ { 𝖠𝖫𝖫 , 𝖴𝖭 } \star\in\{\mathsf{ALL},\mathsf{UN}\} , 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( ( , , , , ) = { D t ¯ ∣ t ¯ ∈ Q ∗ ​ ( D ) } . \mathsf{why}_{\star}((),\hat{D},\hat{Q})\ =\ \{D_{\bar{t}}\mid\bar{t}\in Q^{*}(D)\}. Moreover, for two distinct databases D t ¯ , D u ¯ ∈ 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ ​ ( ( , , , , ) D_{\bar{t}},D_{\bar{u}}\in\mathsf{why}_{\star}((),\hat{D},\hat{Q}) , the symmetric difference between D t ¯ D_{\bar{t}} and D u ¯ D_{\bar{u}} is of the form Δ ⁡ ( D t ¯ , D u ¯ ) = { P ⁡ ( t ¯ ) , P ⁡ ( u ¯ ) } ∪ Δ ⁡ ( D t ¯ ∖ { P ⁡ ( t ¯ ) } , D u ¯ ∖ { P ⁡ ( u ¯ ) } ) , \Delta(D_{\bar{t}},D_{\bar{u}})\ =\ \{P(\bar{t}),P(\bar{u})\}\cup\Delta(D_{\bar{t}}\setminus\{P(\bar{t})\},D_{\bar{u}}\setminus\{P(\bar{u})\}), and thus, d ⁡ ( D t ¯ , D u ¯ ) = | Δ ⁡ ( D t ¯ , D u ¯ ) | = 2 + 2 ⋅ 𝗁𝖽 ⁡ ( t ¯ , u ¯ ) . d(D_{\bar{t}},D_{\bar{u}})\ =\ |\Delta(D_{\bar{t}},D_{\bar{u}})|\ =\ 2+2\cdot\mathsf{hd}(\bar{t},\bar{u}). The above allows us to conclude the following: Observation 2. For each 𝒮 = { D t ¯ 1 , … , D t ¯ k } ∈ 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ k ​ ( ( , , , , ) \mathcal{S}=\{D_{\bar{t}_{1}},\ldots,D_{\bar{t}_{k}}\}\in\mathsf{why}_{\star}^{k}((),\hat{D},\hat{Q}) , δ ⁡ ( 𝒮 ) = ∑ i , j ∈ [ k ] ​ and ​ i < j ( 2 + 2 ⋅ 𝗁𝖽 ⁡ ( t ¯ i , t ¯ j ) ) = k ⋅ ( k − 1 ) + 2 ⋅ δ ⁡ ( { t ¯ 1 , … , t ¯ k } ) . \delta(\mathcal{{S}})=\sum\limits_{i,j\in[k]\text{ and }i<j}(2+2\cdot\mathsf{hd}(\bar{t}_{i},\bar{t}_{j}))=k\cdot(k-1)+2\cdot\delta(\{\bar{t}_{1},\ldots,\bar{t}_{k}\}). We now proceed with the proof of correctness. Let D D , k k , and d d be an input to 𝖣𝖾𝖼𝗂𝖽𝖾𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖠𝗇𝗌𝗐𝖾𝗋𝗌 \mathsf{DecideDiverseAnswers} . ( ⇒ \Rightarrow ) Assume first that there exists a set 𝒜 ∈ 𝖺𝗇𝗌 k ​ ( D , Q ∗ ) \mathcal{A}\in\mathsf{ans}^{k}(D,Q^{*}) with δ ⁡ ( 𝒜 ) ≥ d \delta(\mathcal{A})\geq d . We argue that 𝖣𝖾𝖼𝗂𝖽𝖾𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖠𝗇𝗌𝗐𝖾𝗋𝗌 \mathsf{DecideDiverseAnswers} accepts with input D D , k k , and d d . Note that by the existence of 𝒜 \mathcal{A} , there also exists 𝒜 ∗ ∈ arg ​ max 𝒜 ∈ 𝖺𝗇𝗌 k ​ ( D , Q ∗ ) ⁡ δ ​ ( 𝒜 ) \mathcal{A}^{*}\in\argmax\limits_{\mathcal{A}\in\mathsf{ans}^{k}(D,Q^{*})}\delta(\mathcal{A}) , and all such 𝒜 ∗ \mathcal{A}^{*} have the same diversity such that δ ⁡ ( 𝒜 ∗ ) ≥ d \delta(\mathcal{A}^{*})\geq d . Let d ∗ = δ ⁡ ( 𝒜 ∗ ) d^{*}=\delta(\mathcal{A}^{*}) . By the existence of 𝒜 \mathcal{A} and Observation 1 , the oracle call does not fail and returns a set 𝒮 ^ ∈ 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ k ​ ( ( , , , , ) \mathcal{\hat{S}}\in\mathsf{why}_{\star}^{k}((),\hat{D},\hat{Q}) . Moreover, by Observations 1 and 2, and the fact that 𝒮 ^ ∈ arg ​ max 𝒮 ∈ 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ k ​ ( ( , , , , ) ⁡ δ ​ ( 𝒮 ) \mathcal{\hat{S}}\in\argmax\limits_{\mathcal{S}\in\mathsf{why}_{\star}^{k}((),\hat{D},\hat{Q})}\delta(\mathcal{S}) , we conclude that δ ⁡ ( 𝒮 ^ ) = k ⋅ ( k − 1 ) + 2 ⋅ d ∗ . \delta(\mathcal{\hat{S}})\ =\ k\cdot(k-1)+2\cdot d^{*}. Since d ∗ ≥ d d^{*}\geq d , we have that δ ⁡ ( 𝒮 ^ ) ≥ k ⋅ ( k − 1 ) + 2 ⋅ d \delta(\mathcal{\hat{S}})\geq k\cdot(k-1)+2\cdot d , and thus, 𝖣𝖾𝖼𝗂𝖽𝖾𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖠𝗇𝗌𝗐𝖾𝗋𝗌 \mathsf{DecideDiverseAnswers} accepts, as needed. ( ⇐ \Leftarrow ) Assume now that there is no set 𝒜 ∈ 𝖺𝗇𝗌 k ​ ( D , Q ∗ ) \mathcal{A}\in\mathsf{ans}^{k}(D,Q^{*}) with δ ⁡ ( 𝒜 ) ≥ d \delta(\mathcal{A})\geq d , i.e., either 𝖺𝗇𝗌 k ​ ( D , Q ∗ ) \mathsf{ans}^{k}(D,Q^{*}) is empty, or 𝖺𝗇𝗌 k ​ ( D , Q ∗ ) \mathsf{ans}^{k}(D,Q^{*}) is not empty but every set 𝒜 ∗ ∈ arg ​ max 𝒜 ∈ 𝖺𝗇𝗌 k ​ ( D , Q ∗ ) ⁡ δ ​ ( 𝒜 ) \mathcal{A}^{*}\in\argmax\limits_{\mathcal{A}\in\mathsf{ans}^{k}(D,Q^{*})}\delta(\mathcal{A}) is such that δ ⁡ ( 𝒜 ∗ ) < d \delta(\mathcal{A}^{*})<d . We argue that 𝖣𝖾𝖼𝗂𝖽𝖾𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖠𝗇𝗌𝗐𝖾𝗋𝗌 \mathsf{DecideDiverseAnswers} rejects with input D D , k k , and d d . If 𝖺𝗇𝗌 k ​ ( D , Q ∗ ) \mathsf{ans}^{k}(D,Q^{*}) is empty then, by Observation 1 , 𝗐𝗁𝗒 ⋆ k ​ ( ( , , , , ) \mathsf{why}_{\star}^{k}((),\hat{D},\hat{Q}) is also empty and the oracle call returns fail , which in turn implies that 𝖣𝖾𝖼𝗂𝖽𝖾𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖠𝗇𝗌𝗐𝖾𝗋𝗌 \mathsf{DecideDiverseAnswers} rejects, as needed. Assume now that 𝖺𝗇𝗌 k ​ ( D , Q ∗ ) \mathsf{ans}^{k}(D,Q^{*}) is not empty, but every 𝒜 ∗ ∈ arg ​ max 𝒜 ∈ 𝖺𝗇𝗌 k ​ ( D , Q ∗ ) ⁡ δ ​ ( 𝒜 ) \mathcal{A}^{*}\in\argmax\limits_{\mathcal{A}\in\mathsf{ans}^{k}(D,Q^{*})}\delta(\mathcal{A}) is such that δ ⁡ ( 𝒜 ∗ ) < d \delta(\mathcal{A}^{*})<d .
