Datalog is a powerful rule-based language that allows us to express complex recursive queries and has found numerous applications over the years. Explaining why a result to a Datalog query is obtained is an essential task towards explainable and transparent data-intensive applications that rely on Datalog. A standard way of explaining a query result is the so-called why-provenance, which provides information about the witnesses to a query result in the form of subsets of the input database that as a whole can be used to derive that result. The state-of-the-art approach for efficiently computing the why-provenance explanations of a certain query result aims at enumerating, without repetitions, the relevant explanations by relying on off-the-shelf SAT solvers. However, whenever the set of explanations is very large, outputting the entire set might be prohibitively expensive. Moreover, it is questionable the practical usefulness of flooding the user with a very large number of explanations, many of them possibly differing only marginally. In this case, one can argue that it would be practically more useful to compute a small, sufficiently diverse subset of the set of why-provenance explanations. The present work initiates the study of the latter problem. In particular, we formalize the problem of interest as an optimization problem, and, after showing that it is highly intractable (it is NP-hard even in data complexity), we investigate whether ILP optimization solvers can be employed towards practical solutions. Our main finding is that this is achievable as long as we keep the requested set of explanations small, or we employ approximation algorithms (with error guarantees). 1. Introduction Datalog has emerged in the 1980s as a logic-based query language from Logic Programming and has been extensively studied since then ( Abiteboul et al., 1995 ) . It essentially extends the language of unions of conjunctive queries, which corresponds to the select-project-join-union fragment of relational algebra, with the important feature of recursion, much needed to express some natural queries. As for any other query language, explaining why a result to a Datalog query is obtained is crucial towards explainable and transparent data-intensive applications. A standard way for providing such explanations to query answers is, among others, the so-called why-provenance ( Buneman et al., 2001 ) . Its essence is to collect all the subsets of the input database that as a whole can be used to derive a certain answer. More precisely, in the case of Datalog queries, the why-provenance of an answer tuple t ¯ \bar{t} is obtained by considering all the possible proof trees T T of the fact Ans ​ ( t ¯ ) \text{\rm Ans}(\bar{t}) , with Ans being the answer predicate of the Datalog query in question, and then collecting all the database facts that label the leaves of T T . Recall that a proof tree of a fact α \alpha w.r.t. a database D D and a set Σ \Sigma of Datalog rules forms a tree-like representation of a derivation process that, starting from D D and executing the rules occurring in Σ \Sigma , produces α \alpha ( Abiteboul et al., 1995 ) . Despite its wide acceptance in theory with numerous theoretical studies (see, e.g., ( Calautti et al., 2024c ; Calautti et al., 2024a ; Damásio et al., 2013 ; Deutch et al., 2014 ; Khamis et al., 2022 ) ), why-provenance for Datalog queries suffers from a crucial weaknesses, namely it is computationally very expensive. This is revealed by the fact that until 2020, although why-provenance for Datalog queries has been proposed decades ago, only a couple of works have considered implementing it for recursive queries ( Zhao et al., 2020 ; Esparza et al., 2014 ) . The more recent work ( Elhalawati et al., 2022 ) by Elhalawati et al. tried to make further progress by focusing on the more practical setting of computing the why-provenance of a given query answer (a.k.a. on-demand why-provenance), instead of computing the why-provenance for all the query answers as done in ( Zhao et al., 2020 ; Esparza et al., 2014 ) . Inspired by ( Elhalawati et al., 2022 ) and the idea of on-demand why-provenance, the authors of ( Calautti et al., 2024b ) pushed the state of affairs even further by focusing on the task of enumerating, without repetitions, the members of why-provenance of a given answer by relying on off-the-shelf SAT solvers. In other words, the approach of ( Calautti et al., 2024b ) builds the why-provenance of a query answer in an incremental fashion, i.e., one explanation at a time, which is much more useful in practice than the one-shot computation of the whole set as done in ( Elhalawati et al., 2022 ) . Furthermore, the authors of ( Calautti et al., 2024b ) attacked another weakness of why-provenanance for Datalog queries, namely it might provide counterintuitive explanations. Indeed, as it has been observed in the literature, there are proof trees that correspond to unnatural derivation processes, e.g., derivations where an atom is derived from itself ( Bourgaux et al., 2022 ) , and it is fair to say that an explanation witnessed via such an unnatural proof tree can be classified as a counterintuitive one as it does not correspond to an intuitive derivation process that can be extracted from the proof tree; this is further discussed in Section 3 . Towards conceptually meaningful explanations, the authors of ( Calautti et al., 2024b ) introduced the class of unambiguous proof trees that, unlike arbitrary proof trees, correspond to conceptually meaningful derivation processes, which in turn ensure the conceptual relevance of the obtained explanations. The essence underlying unambiguous proof trees is that they eliminate any ambiguity on how a certain fact α \alpha is derived, namely α \alpha is derived in a unique way that can be exctracted from its unambiguous proof tree. To the best of our knowledge, the approach of ( Calautti et al., 2024b ) forms the state-of-the-art concerning the effective compution of on-demand why-provenance, with the experimental evaluation of ( Calautti et al., 2024b ) providing very encouraging results. Having said that, it remains questionable the practical usefuleness of flooding the user with an extremely large number of why-provenance explanations of the answer of interest, many of them possibly differing only marginally. One can argue that whenever the set of why-provenance explanations of an answer gets very large, it would be practically more useful to provide an overview by outputting a “representative” subset of the set of explanations. A general discussion on this matter about arbitary problems (not only about on-demand why-provenance) can be found in ( Merkl et al., 2025 ) . Two ways for computing a “representative” subset of the set of why-provenance explanations are the following: Sampling Approach.: Randomly select explanations, similarly to what was done for the problem of computing answers to conjunctive queries ( Arenas et al., 2021 ; Carmeli et al., 2022 ) . Diversity Approach.: Conpute a small “diverse” subset of the set of explanations, similarly to what was done for the problem of computing answers to conjunctive queries ( Arenas et al., 2025 ; Merkl et al., 2025 ) . The present work initiates the study of the problem of computing a “representative” subset of the set of why-provenance explanations by adopting the diversity approach. Let us stress that the diversity approach has been applied to numerous problems related to databases (see, e.g., ( Arenas et al., 2025 ; Deng and Fan, 2014 ; Fan et al., 2024 ; Merkl et al., 2025 ) ) and symbolic AI (see, e.g., ( Eiter et al., 2013 ; Hebrard et al., 2005 ; Ingmar et al., 2020 ; Petit and Trapp, 2015 ) ). Following what was done in the literature in other contexts ( Ingmar et al., 2020 ; Merkl et al., 2025 ) , to properly define our problem of interest, we first need to fix the notion of distance between any two why-provenance explanations and the notion of diversity measure that acts as an aggregator that combines pairwise distances. Having those two notions in place, our problem is naturally defined as an optimization problem that aims to compute a set { D 1 , … , D k } \{D_{1},\ldots,D_{k}\} of k k why-provenance explanations (if such a set exists), for some k > 0 k>0 specifed by the user, that maximizes the value obtained by aggregating, using the diversty measure, the pairwise distances of the computed explanations D 1 , … , D k D_{1},\ldots,D_{k} . Concerning the distance between explanations, we adopt the symmetric difference distance, that is, the number of facts on which two explanations D ′ D^{\prime} and D ′′ D^{\prime\prime} differ, denoted by d ⁡ ( D ′ , D ′′ ) d(D^{\prime},D^{\prime\prime}) . Recall that a why-provenance explanation is a subset of the given database (and thus, a set of facts), which means that we can refer to the symmetric difference of D ′ D^{\prime} and D ′′ D^{\prime\prime} . In other words, d ⁡ ( D ′ , D ′′ ) d(D^{\prime},D^{\prime\prime}) is the cardinality of the set of facts ( D ′ ∖ D ′′ ) ∪ ( D ′′ ∖ D ′ ) (D^{\prime}\setminus D^{\prime\prime})\cup(D^{\prime\prime}\setminus D^{\prime}) . When it comes to the diversity measure, in general, one can adopt any computable function f f of the form ⋃ k > 0 ℕ k ⁡ ( k − 1 ) 2 → ℝ \bigcup_{k>0}\mathbb{N}^{\frac{k(k-1)}{2}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} , that is, a function that, for each k > 0 k>0 , assigns to each tuple of integers ( d 1 , … , d k ⁡ ( k − 1 ) 2 ) \left(d_{1},\ldots,d_{\frac{k(k-1)}{2}}\right) , which are essentially the pairwise distances of k k why-provenance explanations, a real number. Of course, towards practical solutions to our problem of interest, the function f f should be conceptually relevant and efficiently computable (i.e., computable in polynomial time). Concrete such functions that have been considered in the literature are, for example, the sum and min functions that assign to a tuple of integers ( d 1 , … , d k ⁡ ( k − 1 ) 2 ) \left(d_{1},\ldots,d_{\frac{k(k-1)}{2}}\right) the integer d 1 + ⋯ + d k ⁡ ( k − 1 ) 2 d_{1}+\cdots+d_{\frac{k(k-1)}{2}} and min ⁡ { d 1 , … , d k ⁡ ( k − 1 ) 2 } \min\left\{d_{1},\ldots,d_{\frac{k(k-1)}{2}}\right\} , respectively ( Merkl et al., 2025 ) . In this work, we adopt the sum function as one of the most commonly used diversity measures. We can now give a semi-formal definition of the optimization problem of interest; the formal definition is given in Section 4 : PROBLEM : 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} INPUT : A Datalog query Q Q , a database D D , an answer t ¯ {\bar{t}} to Q Q over D D , and an integer k > 0 k>0 OUTPUT : A set { D 1 , … , D k } \{D_{1},\ldots,D_{k}\} of why-provenance explanations of t ¯ \bar{t} w.r.t. D D and Q Q that maximizes ∑ 1 ≤ i < j ≤ k d ⁡ ( D i , D j ) \sum_{1\leq i<j\leq k}d(D_{i},D_{j}) if it exists; otherwise fail The goal of the present work is to study the above problem with the aim of providing effective solutions that can be used in practice. For the sake of completeness, we are interested in both settings where the explanations are obtained from arbitary or unambiguous proof trees. Recall that unambiguous proof trees have been introduced in ( Calautti et al., 2024b ) and correspond to conceptually meaningful derivations processes, which in turn lead to conceptually relevant explanations. The first research question that comes up concerns the complexity of 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} : Question 1. Is 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} tractable or intractable? Our theoretical analysis reveals that we are dealing with a highly intractable optimization problem. In particular, we show that our problem is NP-hard, no matter which class of proof trees we consider (arbitrary or unambiguous), even if the Datalog query is fixed (i.e., in data complexity) and consists of a single Datalog rule. This suggests that for providing practical solutions to our problem we need to exploit existing optimization methods that are able to deal with NP-hard problems. A natural choice is Integer Linear Programming (ILP), which leads to our second research question: Question 2. Can ILP optimization solvers lead to practical solutions for 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} ? The key idea towards an answer to the above question is to cast 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} as an ILP optimization problem Π \Pi in such a way that each diverse set of interest can be exctracted from an optimal solution of Π \Pi . Since there are mutliple ways of achieveing this, we define a general framework that allows us to devise such ILP optimization problems in a uniform way, and present a generic algorithm that exploits this framework for solving our problem. The main technical ingredient of this framework is the notion of ILP encoding of the why-provenance explanations of a query answer, which is essentially a system T T of ILP constraints such that each why-provenance explanation of the answer of interest can be extracted from a solution of T T . Given an ILP encoding T T of some query answer and an integer k > 0 k>0 , we then define the ILP optimization problem Π ⁡ [ T , k ] \Pi[T,k] such that each diverse set of k k why-provenance explanations of the answer to be explained can be extracted from an optimal solution of Π ⁡ [ T , k ] \Pi[T,k] . Thus, any pair ( T , k ) (T,k) , where T T is an ILP encoding of some answer and k > 0 k>0 some integer, immediately leads to the ILP optimization problem Π ⁡ [ T , k ] \Pi[T,k] . Now, once we fix our preferred way of building the ILP encoding, we immediately get an algorithm that solves 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} . In particular, given a Datalog query Q Q , a database D D , an answer t ¯ \bar{t} to Q Q over D D , and an integer k k , the algorithm (i) constructs the ILP optimization problem Π ⁡ [ T , k ] \Pi[T,k] , where T T is build according to the fixed preferred way, (ii) finds an optimal solution μ \mu of Π ⁡ [ T , k ] \Pi[T,k] if it exists (otherwise, it fails) by calling an off-the-shelf ILP optimization solver, and (iii) returns the diverse set of k k why-provenance explanations of t ¯ \bar{t} that can be exctracted from the solution μ \mu of Π ⁡ [ T , k ] \Pi[T,k] . After experimenting with different ILP encodings, we have observed that providing practical solutions to 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} is attainable, no matter whether the explanations are obtained from arbitary or unambiguous proof trees, as long as we ask for small diverse sets of explanations (i.e., when the diversity parameter k k is at most three). On the other hand, all the considered ILP encodings lead to algorithms that exhibit poor scalability w.r.t. the diversity parameter k k , and thus, quickly become infeasible for computing larger diverse sets of explanations. This brings us to our last research question whether we can devise alternative approaches that trade optimality of the computed diverse sets for performamce: Question 3. Can we devise approximation algorithms (with error guarantees) for 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} that perform much faster than the exact algorithms and can deal with larger diverse sets? Towards this direction, we target 2 2 -approximation algorithms for 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} that accept as input a Datalog query Q Q , a database D D , an answer t ¯ \bar{t} to Q Q over D D , and an integer k > 0 k>0 , and produce a set { D 1 ′ , … , D k ′ } \{D^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,D^{\prime}_{k}\} of why-provenance explanations of t ¯ \bar{t} (assuming it exists; otherwise, the algorithm fails) such that ∑ 1 ≤ i < j ≤ k d ⁡ ( D i ′ , D j ′ ) ≥ 1 2 ⋅ ∑ 1 ≤ i < j ≤ k d ⁡ ( D i , D j ) , \sum_{1\leq i<j\leq k}d(D^{\prime}_{i},D^{\prime}_{j})\ \geq\ \frac{1}{2}\cdot\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq k}d(D_{i},D_{j}), where { D 1 , … , D k } \{D_{1},\ldots,D_{k}\} is a set of explanations with maximal diversity, i.e., it maximizes ∑ 1 ≤ i < j ≤ k d ⁡ ( D i , D j ) \sum_{1\leq i<j\leq k}d(D_{i},D_{j}) . Similarly to the exact solutions discussed above, we use the generic framework for constructing ILP optimization problems, which in turn are based on the notion of ILP encoding of the why-provenance explanations of a query answer, to devise a generic 2 2 -approximation algorithm for 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} . After experimenting with the various ILP encodings that underly our exact algorithms, we have concluded that the approximation algorithms are indeed much faster than the exact ones with the runtime being reduced by several orders of magnitude. Even as the diversity parameter k k increases, runtimes remain low, with the vast majority of runs completing well below one second, which is a significant improvement over the exact algorithms. We have also assessed the quality of the approximation algorithms and observed that the approximation ratios remain quite close to one. This tells us that the approximation ratios achieved in practice are generally much better than the theoretical ones. Roadmap. After introducing some preliminary notions in Section 2 and the basics of why-provenace for Datalog in Section 3 , we formally define the optimization problem of interest and analyze its data complexity in Section 4 . The various ILP encodings of why-provenance are given in Section 6 . The experimental evaluation of the exact algorithms is performed and discussed in Section 7 . The generic 2 2 -approximation algorithm for 𝖣𝗂𝗏𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖶𝗁𝗒𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗏𝖾𝗇𝖺𝗇𝖼𝖾 \mathsf{DiverseWhyProvenance} is presented in Section 8 .
